subject: GOV.BR
message: The page title "GOV.BR" says nothing about this page.
ref: html
patch_to: Serviços e Informações do Brasil - GOV.BR
auditor: This is the home page of the federal portal gov.br. Its title 'GOV.BR' is the portal's name, and the h1 'Serviços e Informações do Brasil' and the content are the portal's front door. On a site's home page, the site name identifies the page's subject. Inner pages carry their own topic titles, for example 'Consultar CNPJ' and 'Termo de Uso e Aviso de Privacidade'. A professional audit would not log a home page titled with the site name as a 2.4.2 failure. The suggested title is a nicer wording, not a fix for a failure.
skeptic: This is the home page of the GOV.BR portal (I confirmed live that <title> is 'GOV.BR'). A home page's topic is the site itself, so a title naming the site identifies the page and meets 2.4.2. WCAG does not require a tagline. The patch only adds 'Serviços e Informações do Brasil', which makes the title wordier, not compliant.

The real defect is that the visible 'CPF' is not in the accessible name 'document', which is 2.5.3 Label in Name, not 2.4.6. The 2.4.6 label describes its purpose.

, not in the same sentence, paragraph, list item or table cell, and nothing ties it to the link (no aria-describedby or aria-label). A second, identical 'More...' link on the page goes to a different destination (intro/index#software). Strict 2.4.4 practice (F63, WebAIM checklist) logs this. Only the distant h1 'The Community' argues for a pass. The fix is right.
skeptic:
Arguments against a failure: the link is in the section under h1 'The Community', and a preceding section heading is recognized link context (H80). The paragraph right below it reads 'Additional information about the Debian community'. The destination (intro/index#community) is the 'Debian is a Community' section of the intro page. So 'nothing around it does' is factually wrong. Arguments for a failure: that description is a sibling

with no programmatic tie to the link (F63 territory). Also, 'More...' appears twice on the page with different targets (#community and #software), so in a links list it is ambiguous unless the h1 context is counted. This is a borderline call, not a clear failure either way.

subject: Download
message: The link text "Download" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor: The 'Download' button sits under h1 'The Operating System' and h2 'Debian is a complete Free Operating System!', in a container next to the logo img alt='Debian'. The preceding heading (H80) makes its purpose clear: download Debian. It is the only plain 'Download' link on the page, and it does go straight to the current Debian installer image. 2.4.4 does not require the version or file format in the link text. 'Nothing around it does' is wrong, and the patch only adds detail.
skeptic: The 'Download' button sits in the block under h1 'The Operating System' and the immediately preceding h2 'Debian is a complete Free Operating System!'. It shares a container with the Debian logo (alt 'Debian') and an 'Other downloads' link. Link text plus the preceding heading (H80) gives the purpose: download Debian. The claim that nothing around it helps is false. 2.4.4 does not require the link text to name the exact ISO variant or version, so the patch only rewords a link that already meets the criterion.

subject: More...
message: The link text "More..." does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

that is not tied to the link. The link shares the text 'More...' with another link that goes to a different destination (intro/index#community). The purpose cannot be determined from the link text plus programmatically determined context, so a strict audit logs it under 2.4.4.

This is the same pattern as the community 'More...' link. Arguments against a failure: it sits under h1 'The Operating System' (section-heading context, H80). subject: the default document language
message: The link text "the default document language" does not match where the link leads: a page titled "Debian -- Debian Website in different Languages".

It goes to ./intro/cn, 'Debian Website in different Languages'. That page explains content negotiation: how to set the browser's language preference and override it with a cookie. That is exactly what the link text plus its context promises. A link does not have to repeat the destination's title, so the mismatch claim is wrong.

It goes to ./intro/cn, 'Debian Website in different Languages', which is the content-negotiation page explaining how to set the browser's language preference for the site. Link text plus its sentence describes that destination exactly. The model compared the bare link text with the page title and ignored the sentence. The patch would remove the meaningful 'how to set' purpose.

subject: More...

Arguments for a failure: the heading text itself names no topic, and the page has two identical 'More...' h2s that look the same in a headings list. It is a weak heading, but whether it fails 2.4.6 depends on how much the parent heading counts.

subject: Name *
message: The field "Name *" asks for the user's full name but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="name" is missing.
ref: #realname
auditor: #realname is the visible, required 'Name *' field of a support form; it collects the user's own name (an Input Purposes entry, 'name') and has no autocomplete attribute (confirmed in snapshot and live HTML). Missing autocomplete on a user-information field is a standard 1.3.5 failure (technique H98 not met).
skeptic: #realname is the visible 'Name *' field of a support form that asks for the user's own name. Its markup (<input type="text" id="realname" name="realname" required>) has no autocomplete attribute, so its purpose is not programmatically identified. autocomplete="name" is the matching input purpose from the WCAG list. This fails 1.3.5.

subject: Website *
message: The field "Website *" asks for the user's website, but autocomplete="off" does not identify that purpose.
ref: #website
auditor: #website is a spam honeypot, not a field for the user: its row is styled position:absolute;left:-9999px;top:-9999px;height:0;width:0;overflow:hidden (site CSS 'form .row.website'), the input has tabindex=-1 and autocomplete=off, and it is not required. It is not meant to collect information about the user, so 1.3.5 does not apply. The suggested autocomplete=url would invite autofill and break the trap. The snapshot showed the offscreen state and tabindex=-1, so the model had what it needed and misread the element.
skeptic: #website is a spam honeypot, not a field that collects information about the user. Its label and the input sit at x/y -9999 (snapshot state 'offscreen'), it has tabindex=-1 and autocomplete=off, and it does not appear in the screenshot. 1.3.5 only covers inputs that collect information about the user, and people are meant to leave this one empty. The suggested autocomplete="url" would make browsers fill the trap and get real users flagged as spam.

subject: Email Address *
message: The field "Email Address *" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing.
ref: #email
auditor: #email is the visible, required 'Email Address *' field and collects the user's own email (Input Purposes 'email'). It has type=email but no autocomplete attribute (confirmed live). type=email does not identify the purpose per H98, and auditors routinely log missing autocomplete=email as a 1.3.5 failure.
skeptic: #email asks for the user's own email address: the helper text says 'otherwise, we will not be able to respond to you'. It has type="email" but no autocomplete attribute. Under 1.3.5, type=email only sets the input format. It does not say the address belongs to the user, which is what autocomplete="email" does. Leaving autocomplete out fails 1.3.5.

subject: Website *
message: Nothing on screen tells what to enter in the field "Website *": its label is hidden from view.
ref: #website
auditor: The same honeypot #website is deliberately hidden offscreen and removed from the tab order; it does not ask sighted users for input, so 3.3.2 (labels or instructions when content requires user input) does not apply. It also has a programmatic label <label for=website>. The suggested visible label would expose the trap and cause real users to fill it. A real concern does exist (the honeypot stays in the accessibility tree as 'Website *', so screen reader users may reach it), but it is a different issue with the opposite fix (hide it from AT or label it 'leave blank'), not the missing visible label claimed here.
skeptic: #website is a hidden honeypot (offscreen at -9999, tabindex=-1, autocomplete=off, not shown in the screenshot). 3.3.2 applies when content requires user input, and this field is meant to stay empty. It already has a programmatic label, <label for="website">Website *</label>, hidden offscreen together with the input, so the suggested patch adds a duplicate of a label that already exists. Exposing a honeypot to screen readers can be an accessibility problem, but it is not a missing label or instructions under 3.3.2.

subject: example image

The sentence right before it says 'Consider this image of Ellen Ochoa:', and the Note right after it says that most images in the article deliberately have alt="example image" and that their content is given in the page text. The image's content is named next to it, so a screen reader user loses nothing important. The claim that the alt 'describes something the image does not show' is also wrong: the alt describes nothing at all, and the image really is an example. Rampa's 1.1.1 judge only gets ancestor text, so it saw neither the sentence before the image nor the Note.

The text right before it says 'Consider this image of Ellen Ochoa:', and the Note right after it (#context > div:nth-of-type(1) > p) says 'most images within this article have been given alt="example image". However, the content of the images is typically presented within page context.' Later text adds 'Her mode of dress further conveys that she is an astronaut.' So the placeholder alt is deliberate and documented, and the surrounding text gives the content. Also, the claim that 'example image' describes something the image does not show is false: it is accurate as far as it goes.

Her mode of dress further conveys that she is an astronaut'), and the section's Note explains the alt="example image" placeholder. Then it gives the answer: alt="Astronaut Ellen Ochoa". 1.1.1's test/exercise provision covers this case. If the image had the full text alternative, the answer would be given away, so a text alternative that only identifies the image is enough. The page documents that 'example image' is used for this reason, and the body text describes the content (Ellen Ochoa, dressed as an astronaut). The patch is in fact the answer to the exercise.

subject: example image

The same documented placeholder convention and test/exercise provision apply, and 'Ellen Ochoa, Astronaut' follows right after the link. However, unlike the other examples, the image is the only content of a live link to en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ellen_Ochoa. Its accessible name, 'example image', conveys none of the link's function, for example to a user navigating by links. The exercise framing may not fully excuse that. The stated reason ('describes something the image does not show') is wrong either way, and the patch describes appearance rather than function.

subject: Select or type your state or territory:

A user can pick any state, not just their home state. 1.3.5 covers inputs that collect information about the user, and a typical audit would not log a state picker for finding content. address-level1 autofill would also not fill this custom list correctly. subject: image unavailable
message: The text alternative "image unavailable" describes something the image does not show.
ref: #bbc-main > article > div:nth-of-type(6) > div > div > div > div > figure > div > img:nth-of-type(1)
patch_to: A street stall featuring a photograph of a woman, umbrellas, and red berries.
auditor: This img is BBC's lazy-load stand-in (src grey-placeholder.png, aria-label 'image unavailable'). The real photo is its next sibling, with alt "A photo of Maricarmen Abascal at Madrid's Puerta del Sol" and a figcaption. On the live page the placeholder is only in the DOM until the real image loads, and then it is removed. Before that it is shown as a grey box. So the photo's text alternative is provided by its own img, and the placeholder's label matches what the placeholder shows. The vision crop at these bounds showed the sibling photo painted on top, which led the model to judge the placeholder against the photo. Putting a photo description on the placeholder would only repeat the sibling's alt. At most this is a best-practice note to aria-hide the placeholder, not a 1.1.1 failure for a missing alt for the photo.
skeptic: This img is BBC's lazy-load stand-in (src grey-placeholder.png, class hide-when-no-script). It sits under the real photo img:nth-of-type(2), which has the same bounds and alt "A photo of Maricarmen Abascal at Madrid's Puerta del Sol". The placeholder is pure decoration, but it is exposed as role=img with aria-label "image unavailable", so a screen reader announces a false 'image unavailable' before the real photo. 1.1.1 requires decoration to be ignorable by assistive technology (F39: non-null alt on an image that should be ignored), so this element does fail. The finding's diagnosis is wrong, though. Its crop showed the overlapping real photo. The patch, which gives the placeholder a description of that photo, would only duplicate the sibling's alt. The fix is alt="" or aria-hidden="true" on the placeholder.

auditor: This is the video thumbnail link (a.feed-post-figure-link). Besides the '1 min' duration it holds an img with alt="Lago na Turquia tem minerais iguais aos de antigo lago em Marte - Programa: G1 Ciência e Saúde ". That img is not aria-hidden and has no presentation role, and the snapshot records the alt on the img node. In the live page, Edge's accessibility tree (CDP getPartialAXTree) computes the link's name from its contents as 'Lago na Turquia tem minerais iguais aos de antigo lago em Marte - Programa: G1 Ciência e Saúde 1 min'. That name alone describes the destination, a video page titled 'Vídeo: Lago na Turquia tem minerais iguais aos de antigo lago em Marte'. The snapshot recorded the name as '1 min' because the collector's accessibleName() in src/surfaces/in-page.ts uses el.textContent for links and leaves out img alt text inside the link. The model judged that wrong name. On top of that, the h2 link with the same headline and the same href comes just before it in the same feed-post. The suggested patch would also drop the image and replace the current name with a weaker one. Not a 2.4.4 failure.

The link's real accessible name is not '1 min'. The wraps plus the duration

1 min

. No aria-hidden or role=presentation is set, and the image is rendered: the snapshot's readingText for the cover div includes the alt, and the screenshot shows the thumbnail. Under accname, a link's name from content includes a child img's alt. So browsers and screen readers announce 'Lago na Turquia tem minerais iguais aos de antigo lago em Marte - Programa: G1 Ciência e Saúde 1 min'. That names the destination, whose title is 'Vídeo: Lago na Turquia tem minerais...'. The snapshot recorded '1 min' because the collector's accessibleName (src/surfaces/in-page.ts:208) uses el.textContent, which drops img alt. Even with a bare '1 min', the claim that nothing around it helps is false. The same feed-post card has an h2 just before it holding a link with the same href and the text 'Lago na Turquia tem minerais iguais aos de antigo lago em Marte' (H80 context). auditor: This is the visible desktop logo (275x52 at 1280px). It is the only content of the header link to the home page; the mobile variant is hidden. subject: Saiba mais
message: The link text "Saiba mais" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.
ref: #cidades-estados-link-bottom
auditor: "Saiba mais" is the button-styled link that closes the home page's "Cidades e Estados" module. It goes to /cidades-e-estados.html?c=4205407, the Cidades e Estados page for the municipality shown. The link sits in the same container as the h2 "Cidades e Estados", which precedes it. In between are the selected city, "Florianópolis ( SC ) - 4205407", and that city's population, area and code (snapshot and screenshot). Under H80, the link text combined with the preceding heading ("Saiba mais" + "Cidades e Estados") describes the purpose: more on this city in Cidades e Estados. That is programmatically determined link context, which is enough for 2.4.4 (Level A). The finding's claim that "nothing around it does" is wrong, and the packet gave the model that heading. Link text on its own would only be required by 2.4.9 (AAA). The live page now shows another capital (Brasília), but the structure is the same.
skeptic: "Saiba mais" is the button-styled link at the bottom of the "Cidades e Estados" block and points to /cidades-e-estados.html?c=4205407. The finding says nothing around it gives its purpose, and that is wrong. The closest heading before it is the h2 "Cidades e Estados". Between that heading and the link are the place selector showing "Florianópolis ( SC ) - 4205407" and Florianópolis's population, area and municipal code (4205407, the same code as in the href). Under technique H80 (link text plus the preceding heading), "Saiba mais" in the "Cidades e Estados" section identifies the destination: the Cidades e Estados page for the place shown. 2.4.4 accepts programmatically determined context, so this passes even though "Saiba mais sobre Florianópolis" would be clearer. The heading and the block text were in the checker's context (headingsNear, ancestors), so the misjudgement is the model's.

subject: English
message: "English" is in English, but it inherits the page's language (pt-BR): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="en" to the link.
ref: html > body > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
auditor: The element is the language-switcher link to /en/home-eng.html in the header. It contains only a flag image with alt="English" and title="English". The page is lang="pt-BR", and neither the link nor the image has lang="en" (confirmed in the snapshot and the live HTML). The 3.1.2 Understanding document's own example ("Alternative language links") shows links that each name their language in that language and are marked with a lang attribute. The word is clearly meant to be in English, would be pronounced differently by a Portuguese voice, and is not part of Portuguese vernacular, so the single-word and vernacular exceptions do not apply. Adding lang="en" on the link, as the patch does, fixes it. Rampa's low confidence is understandable, but the failure is real.
skeptic: The link to /en/home-eng.html holds only a UK flag img whose alt and title are "English". Neither the img nor the link has a lang attribute, so the text inherits html lang="pt-BR" (checked in the snapshot root and on the live page). I tried the exceptions. The 3.1.2 Understanding note about single words being part of the surrounding language does not apply, because the change of language is clearly intended here. "English" is not Portuguese vernacular (Portuguese says "Inglês"). The Understanding document's own "Alternative language links" example treats language names in a switcher as needing lang. The text alternative is content, so H58's test fails for the img. No technique or context makes this pass.

subject: Buscar
message: The placeholder "Buscar" has a contrast of 4.08:1 with the field (#757575 on #f1f1f1). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
ref: html > body > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > form > input
auditor: The element is the visible desktop header search field, with placeholder "Buscar". The site CSS sets the field background to #f1f1f1 (input.header__busca--campo), sets no placeholder colour, and uses 16px italic weight 500. That leaves Chrome's default placeholder colour, #757575. Sampling the screenshot inside the field gives a #f1f1f1 background with #757575 glyph cores. The contrast is 4.08:1, which I recomputed. That is below 4.5:1, and the text is not large. The 1.4.3 Understanding document says the criterion covers placeholder text. The field is enabled, so the inactive-component exception does not apply. The placeholder is also the only visible label, because the real label has font-size 0.
skeptic: This is the header search field's placeholder "Buscar" (16px, weight 500, normal-size text). The darkest glyph pixel in the screenshot is #757575 on a #f1f1f1 field, and live computed styles today give the same rgb(117,117,117) on rgb(241,241,241). That is 4.08:1, below 4.5:1. The placeholder is not incidental: the <label> has font-size:0, so the placeholder and the icon are the only visible cues for the field. The strongest counter-argument is G174: the page has a high-contrast toggle (#setConstrast), and in that mode the placeholder is #757575 on #000, 4.56:1. But the toggle is an <a> with no href. A live Tab test in Edge skips it, going from the logo link straight to the language links, and it is exposed as a generic element rather than a control. A mechanism that only pointer users can reach cannot count as conforming, so the default view's failure stands.

subject: Buscar Buscar
message: The label "Buscar Buscar" does not say what to enter.
ref: html > body > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > form > input
auditor: The element is the header site-search field, next to a magnifier button named "Buscar". The live HTML has <label for="mod-search-searchword">Buscar</label>. The computed name "Buscar Buscar" comes from a duplicate id: the hidden mobile header repeats the same form, and both labels point at the first input. So the patch's "before" HTML, which shows label text "Buscar Buscar", is not the real markup. Either way, "Buscar" (Search) on a search field in the site header is a standard label that describes the field's purpose: site search. 2.4.6 requires no more than that. The doubled word is redundancy from the duplicate ids, a markup/name-computation issue arguably under 4.1.2, not a label that fails to describe the purpose.
skeptic: The accessible name "Buscar Buscar" comes from two <label for="mod-search-searchword">Buscar</label> elements. The second sits in the hidden mobile header and reuses the same id, so both labels attach to the desktop input. Each label just says "Buscar" (Search), and the patch's claimed label text "Buscar Buscar" does not exist. For a site search field in the page header, "Buscar" describes its purpose and what to type, which is all 2.4.6 asks. The doubled name is a duplicate-id quirk, not a non-descriptive label. Wanting the label to spell out more ("Pesquisar no site") is stricter than 2.4.6. The duplicate ids and the font-size:0 label could matter for other criteria, but not for this one.

subject: Español
message: "Español" is in Spanish, but it inherits the page's language (en): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="es" to the link.
ref: #header > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a
auditor: The element is the header language switcher, Español, on a page whose only language declaration is . The snapshot and the live HTML (fetched 2026-10-09, unchanged from the run) show no lang attribute on the link or on any ancestor. hreflang only describes the linked resource and does not set the language of the link text, so 'Español' is programmatically English. The word is the Spanish name of the language, used on purpose to point to the Spanish version, so the change of language is clearly intended. It is not a proper name, technical term or English loanword, so the single-word and vernacular exceptions do not apply. The Understanding document for 3.1.2 uses this exact pattern as its 'Alternative language links' example, with lang on each link. The finding's claim and its fix (lang="es" on the link) are correct.
skeptic: The element is the header language switcher, Español, on a page with . The snapshot shows no lang on the link or on any ancestor other than html, and the live HTML I fetched on 2026-10-09 is the same, so the page has not changed. I looked for reasons it could pass. hreflang only gives the language of the linked resource, not of the link text, so it does not meet H58. The proper-name exception does not apply: Understanding 3.1.2 has an 'Alternative language links' example of exactly this pattern (Deutsch, Français...) and says each link's language is indicated with a lang attribute. The single-word guidance ('single words should be considered part of the language of the surrounding text unless it is clear that a change in language was intended') does not save it either. The change is clearly intended: the label is the language's own name, addressed to Spanish readers, and the author's hreflang shows awareness of it. The word, with its ñ, is not pronounced the same under English rules, and it is not an adopted English word like 'rendezvous'. Role=button is irrelevant to this criterion. No reason holds up, so this fails 3.1.2 as the finding says, and the patch (lang="es" on the link) is the right fix.

subject: Earth
message: The link text "Earth" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.
ref: #bbc-footer > section:nth-of-type(1) > nav > ul > li:nth-of-type(10) > div > a
auditor: The element is the "Earth" link (href /future-planet) in the BBC site footer, a list item inside <nav aria-label="Footer navigation"> next to Home, News, Sport, Business, Technology, Health, Culture, Arts, Travel, Audio, Video, Live and Weather. Under 2.4.4 (In Context), the link's list item and the labelled navigation landmark are its programmatically determined context. In a list of site sections, "Earth" clearly names the BBC Earth section, and that is where it goes: the destination's title is "BBC Earth" and its heading is "Earth". Section names in a site navigation menu are a standard passing pattern, and a professional auditor would not fail this link. The checker had the ancestors and the destination and still judged it wrongly.
skeptic: The element is the "Earth" link (href /future-planet) in the BBC footer's "Footer navigation" list: Home, News, Sport, Business, Technology, Health, Culture, Arts, Travel, Earth, Audio, Video, Live, Weather. The same "Earth" link to /future-planet is also in the page's main navigation bar at the top. In a site section menu, a link named after a section identifies its purpose: it goes to the BBC's Earth section. The destination Rampa fetched confirms this. Its h1 is "Earth" and its title is "BBC Earth | Environment, Climate Change...", so the link text matches the destination heading exactly. The nav list is programmatically determined context for the link (G53/G91 territory), and the link text alone already describes the destination, so 2.4.4 is met. The packet gave the model the nav ancestors and the destination heading, so this is a judgment error, not missing context. The suggested 'BBC Earth' rename is cosmetic, and the finding's claim that 'nothing around it' says where the link goes is wrong.

subject: TikTok for Business
message: The link text "TikTok for Business" is shared by 3 links that lead to 3 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: #google_ads_iframe_\/95377733\/tvg_G1\/Ciencia\.Home_0 |> #banner > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a
auditor: This is the advertiser display-URL link 'TikTok for Business' in the Google Ad Manager banner iframe (Home_0, iframe aria-label 'Publicidade'). The three 'TikTok for Business' / 'TIKTOK FOR BUSINESS' links are the same TikTok ad served in three slots (Home_0, Home_4, Home_5). Their doubleclick click-tracking hrefs differ only in tracking parameters, and all carry the same adurl, ads.tiktok.com/business/pt-BR/industries/cpg. So they do not lead to 3 different places. The link text names its destination (TikTok for Business), so its purpose can be determined from the link text alone. Identical text across links is at most a best-practice concern in Understanding 2.4.4, not a failure. The checker had the hrefs and read different tracking URLs as different destinations.
skeptic: This is the 'TikTok for Business' link in the Google ad banner iframe Home_0. The other two links with this name are the 'TIKTOK FOR BUSINESS' links in the tower ads Home_4 and Home_5, which show the same TikTok creative. I decoded the adurl parameter of each href in the snapshot. All three lead to the same landing page, https://ads.tiktok.com/business/pt-BR/industries/cpg, with the same campaign parameters. The hrefs differ only in Google click-tracking tokens (ai, sig, cid, gclid), so 'lead to 3 different places' is wrong. The link text names the advertiser and describes the purpose on its own. Identical text with an equivalent purpose does not fail 2.4.4, and even the AAA identical-name rules would pass it. Rampa had the hrefs, adurl included, and treated tracking redirects as different destinations.

subject: Abrir
message: The link text "Abrir" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.
ref: #google_ads_iframe_\/95377733\/tvg_G1\/Ciencia\.Home_0 |> #banner > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(3) > a
auditor: This is the 'Abrir' (Open) call-to-action link in the TikTok banner ad iframe (Home_0). Its accessible name is only 'Abrir', with no aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby or title. In the snapshot it sits in a bare div next to the 'TikTok for Business' link: no enclosing paragraph, sentence, list item or table cell gives programmatically determined context (H77/H78/H79/G53/ARIA7/ARIA8 are not met). The iframe name 'Publicidade' says only that it is an ad. Sighted users see it as the ad's CTA, so the 'ambiguous to users in general' exception does not apply. 'Abrir' alone does not convey the link's purpose, so it fails 2.4.4 (the ACT 'link in context is descriptive' reading). This is third-party ad content, but it is part of the page and no partial-conformance statement exists. Some auditors would accept the ad unit as context, but the strict and usual reading fails it. The suggested patch invents a destination description, but that does not change the label.
skeptic: This is the 'Abrir' CTA in the Home_0 ad banner, in an iframe labelled 'Publicidade'. The claim that nothing around it tells where it goes is doubtful. In the snapshot it shares a row container (readingText 'TikTok for Business Abrir') with the adjacent 'TikTok for Business' link, which goes to the same landing page. The rest of the ad ('Cadastre-se no TikTok', the description) is in the same small ad document, and the screenshot shows 'TikTok for Business ... Abrir >' on one line. But the context sits in generic divs, not in a paragraph, list item, table cell, aria-describedby or aria-labelledby. That is not one of the relationships the 2.4.4 Understanding document and techniques H77/H78/H79/G53/ARIA7/ARIA8 name. Strict auditors would fail the generic 'Abrir'; others would accept the self-contained ad card as its context. Competent auditors would disagree, so it is not a clear true positive.

That context is only in sibling generic divs, though, not in a sentence, paragraph, list item, table cell or ARIA relationship, the forms that 2.4.4's Understanding text and techniques name as programmatically determined link context. Whether a self-contained ad card counts as context is something competent auditors would disagree on. 'Abrir' alone is generic, but the claim is not clearly a failure.

subject: Search
message: Nothing on screen says what to enter in this field: its label is hidden from view ("Search"), and no text, button or legend sits near it.
ref: #search
auditor: This is the desktop header search field (#search). Its aria-labelledby points to #searchBtn, a submit button that sits inside the right end of the field and shows a magnifying-glass icon (fa-search), with 'Search' as sr-only text. The screenshot confirms the icon is visible. WCAG defines a label as text or another component with a text alternative, and G167 (an adjacent button that labels the field's purpose) is a sufficient technique for 3.3.2. A search box with a magnifying-glass submit button in the site header is the standard case that technique covers. The finding's claim that 'no text, button or legend sits near it' is wrong. The rule required visible text and ignored the icon button, which is stricter than 3.3.2. The live markup is unchanged.
skeptic: This is the header search field (#search). The screenshot and snapshot show a visible magnifying-glass submit button (#searchBtn, accessible name 'Search') at the right end of the field, inside the same search form. The input takes its name from that button through aria-labelledby. This is sufficient technique G167, whose Example 1 is exactly a search field labelled by an adjacent magnifying-glass button, so 3.3.2 is met. The rule's claim that no button sits near the field is wrong given the data it had.

subject: turn UP the TERROR!
message: The link text "turn UP the TERROR!" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.
ref: html > body > site-messages > div > div > div > a
auditor:
This is the link 'turn UP the TERROR!' in the site-wide promo banner. The live markup is unchanged: '
The Halloween countdown has begun ... Are you ready to turn UP the TERROR!?
'. The link goes to the Halloween 2026 shopping guides page. Under 2.4.4 (in context), the enclosing sentence and message block are programmatically determined context (G53). That context tells the user the link leads to Adafruit's Halloween content. Screen-reader users get the same context sighted users get, and any ambiguity left over is ambiguous to all users, which the criterion exempts. The finding's claim that 'nothing around it' tells where the link goes is wrong. Vaguer marketing link text like this is at most a 2.4.9 (AAA) concern.
skeptic: The link 'turn UP the TERROR!' sits in the orange Halloween alert banner. Its parent div.message reads 'The Halloween countdown has begun ... Are you ready to turn UP the TERROR!?', and the banner has role=alert, so the whole message is read with the link. That parent text is programmatically determined link context. Together with the link text, it tells the user the link leads to the Halloween promotion, and it does: the destination is 'Halloween 2026 : Shopping Guides'. The finding's claim that 'nothing around it' says where the link goes is contradicted by the ancestor text Rampa itself captured. The link text is vague on its own, but 2.4.4 accepts context, so this passes. Judged on the 2026-10-10 snapshot; the seasonal banner may change on the live site.

subject: unmarked|pt-BR|to overwrite the file?', 2, 'Come on, only yes or
message: This passage has no lang attribute, so it is read as Brazilian Portuguese (pt-BR), but it is in English (en).
ref: #default-argument-values > ul > li:nth-of-type(3) > p
auditor: The element is a list-item paragraph in a page marked html lang="pt-BR": "ou fornecendo todos os argumentos:" followed by the inline code sample ask_ok('OK to overwrite the file?', 2, 'Come on, only yes or no!'). The live HTML confirms there is no lang attribute anywhere except on the html element. The translator left the code's string literals in English, even though the function defined just above uses Portuguese strings (pergunta_ok, 'Por favor, tente novamente!'). Those literals are real English phrases, not proper names, technical terms or vernacular words, and a pt-BR speech synthesizer would mispronounce them. A strict reading of 3.1.2 makes this a failure. But they are part of a Python code sample in a code element: WCAG defines human language as language used to communicate with humans, and the 3.1.2 Understanding document says nothing about code samples. Many auditors treat code as outside the criterion, so competent auditors would reasonably disagree. Rampa's evidence and patch wrap only a fragment of the string, which is a weak fix but does not settle the label.
skeptic: The passage is inline <code> in a pt-BR page (html lang="pt-BR", no lang on the code, confirmed in the live HTML): ask_ok('OK to overwrite the file?', 2, 'Come on, only yes or no!'). The English words are real human-language string literals that a Portuguese voice would mispronounce, which supports the finding. But the whole thing is a Python call expression, and the quoted span runs across code syntax ("', 2, '"). WCAG defines human language as language used to communicate with humans. Neither 3.1.2's Understanding document nor its techniques say whether code samples, or string literals inside them, need marking. Auditors differ in practice: many treat code as exempt, others would want lang="en" on the code. With no clear normative answer, this could be a real failure or out of scope, so it is uncertain.

subject: An arm wears a unique device like a sleeve connected to wires
message: The text alternative "An arm wears a unique device like a sleeve connected to wires" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: #main > div > article > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > figure > a > img
auditor: The large spotlight image (img.spotlight__img) is the only content of an <a> that goes to the news.mit.edu story on the shape-sensing sheet. Its alt, "An arm wears a unique device like a sleeve connected to wires", describes the picture, so the link's accessible name does not say that it opens the full story. The live HTML (re-fetched 2026-10-09) is unchanged. The Understanding document for 1.1.1 treats linked images under Controls (Situation C, H30), and its own examples (a newspaper thumbnail with alt "Smallville Times", a globe with alt "International Travel") give alt text that names the destination. H30's test fails here. A "Full story" link with the same href comes later, after the h2 and the paragraph. It is a separate link, not combined with the image link as H2 would do, so the image link is still announced with no purpose. The patch is acceptable. Combining the two links, or removing the redundant image link from the tab order and the accessibility tree, would also fix it.
skeptic: The spotlight hero image is the only content of a link (target=_blank) to the news story about a shape-sensing sheet. The live HTML on 2026-10-09 matches the snapshot. The link has no aria-label or title, and it is not hidden with aria-hidden or tabindex=-1, so its name is the alt, which describes the picture (an arm in a wired sleeve) and not the story it opens. I looked for reasons it could pass. The only other link to the same URL is a vague "Full story" link, placed after the h2 and the paragraph, so it is not an adjacent H2-style duplicate that would carry the purpose. The name is computed correctly, so this is not a collector artefact. 1.1.1 Situation C (G82/H30) requires an image that is a link's only content to describe the link's purpose, and this alt fails H30's test step 2. That is WCAG's own rule, not a stricter one.

subject: Students engaged in math and in a maker space

ref: #main > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > img
auditor: This is a card image whose only content is an img inside an <a> to the news.mit.edu article on the MIT for America initiative. The alt "Students engaged in math and in a maker space" describes the photo (confirmed in the crop) and does not say that the link opens the MIT for America story. The h3 link "MIT for America" next to it has the same href, but it is a separate anchor in a sibling div, so it is not the image link's name. The two are not combined per H2, and the image link is not hidden from AT or the tab order. That fails H30 / Situation C of 1.1.1: a functional image's text alternative should convey its purpose, as in the Understanding document's linked-thumbnail example. The live page is unchanged. Some auditors would log this under 2.4.4 instead, but the 1.1.1 claim as stated holds.
skeptic: This card image is the only content of a link to the news story "MIT for America initiative strengthens STEM education". The live page matches the snapshot. The alt "Students engaged in math and in a maker space" describes the photo. It is on the same broad theme (students, STEM) but does not tell a user that the link opens the MIT for America story. The strongest reason against the finding is that the h3 link "MIT for America" right below goes to the same URL (the redundant pattern in H2). H2 treats separate adjacent links as a redundancy problem and does not excuse the image link's own name. The image link is still a separate tab stop and links-list entry, and its name does not state its purpose. No aria-label, title or hiding technique applies, so H30/G82 (1.1.1 Situation C) is not met. The patch's wording may not be ideal, but that does not change the label.

subject: a man wearing an Encora device while eating soup
message: The text alternative "a man wearing an Encora device while eating soup" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: #main > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > img
auditor: This is a card image whose only content is an img inside an <a> to the news.mit.edu story on Encora Therapeutics' FDA-cleared tremor treatment. The alt "a man wearing an Encora device while eating soup" describes the scene. It names the device but reads as a photo description and does not say that the link opens the "Treating tremors" story. The adjacent h3 link with the same href is a separate anchor, so the image link is announced on its own with a name that does not describe its purpose. That fails H30 / Situation C of 1.1.1 (linked images need alt text that conveys the destination). H2, combining the links, would be the cleaner fix. The live markup is unchanged.
skeptic: This card image is the only content of a link to the story about the FDA clearing the Encora tremor device. The live page matches the snapshot. The alt "a man wearing an Encora device while eating soup" describes the photo, but it names the product the linked story is about. A fair reading can say a user can tell the link leads to content about the Encora device, which is the least 1.1.1 asks: that the user knows what the control is and why it is there. The h3 link "Treating tremors" right below goes to the same URL (the H2 pattern), so the purpose is stated in the next link. A strict H30 reading would still say the alt describes the image, not the link's function, and it does not say the link opens a news story. With the destination's subject named and an adjacent duplicate link, I think competent auditors would disagree.

subject: Braedon Rudolph
message: The text alternative "Braedon Rudolph" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: #main > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > img
auditor: This is a card image whose only content is an img inside an <a> to an MIT Spectrum (betterworld.mit.edu) profile, "From MIT to the Marines", about Braedon Rudolph '26. Its alt is "Braedon Rudolph". The pattern is the same as the other cards: a separate adjacent h3 link with the same href, not combined per H2. Unlike the others, though, the alt names the subject of the destination: a link called "Braedon Rudolph" that opens a profile of Braedon Rudolph arguably does tell the user where it leads, much like the Understanding document's "Smallville Times" example. It does not say the link is an article or story, and it was written as a photo caption (the crop shows several graduates). Competent auditors could reasonably differ on whether this name describes the link's purpose well enough for 1.1.1 / H30, so I leave it uncertain. The live page is unchanged.
skeptic: This card image is the only content of a link to the Spectrum profile of Braedon Rudolph ("After MIT, the Marines"). The live page matches the snapshot. The alt "Braedon Rudolph" does not describe the photo, which shows a group of graduates. It works as a label naming the person the linked article is about. Like H30's example alt "Current routes at Boulders Climbing Gym", which names the destination's content, a link named after a person who is the subject of the destination arguably does describe its purpose. The h3 link "From MIT to the Marines" right below goes to the same URL. A strict auditor would still say "Braedon Rudolph" does not say the link opens a story. The finding's claim that the alt "does not say where the link leads" is contestable here, so I label it uncertain rather than true_positive.

The alt "Kilian Court at MIT" names the place in the photo and has nothing to do with the destination, so a user who meets the link out of context would expect a page about Kilian Court. The adjacent h3 link to the same URL reduces the impact but does not satisfy the requirement for this separate control. No technique (aria-label, title, hiding the redundant link) makes it pass, and the snapshot data is correct. This fails 1.1.1 for controls (G82/H30) as the finding says. The patch's alt text ("Visit the MIT Understanding page") is awkward, but that does not change the label.

subject: PythOnRio
message: The text alternative "PythOnRio" describes something the image does not show.
ref: html > body > div > main > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(8) > img
auditor: This is the logo slot in the PythOnRio card of the user-group grid. The src is the site's placeholder images/comunidades-locais/default.png, a plain Python logo. The template puts the group name in every card's alt: the snapshot and the live page (unchanged) show the same default.png with alt set to the group name on 11 cards (GruPy-MT, Py013, PyTche, PythOnRio, and others). In the card the image stands in for the group's logo, right under the h4 "PythOnRio". The alt names the group, which is the job the image does there. A sighted user gets no information from the generic logo that a screen reader user misses, apart from the fact that the group has no logo of its own. Strictly, the image is redundant or decorative and alt="" would be better practice. But a redundant name is not a 1.1.1 failure, and the alt is not a placeholder or file name (F30). The finding requires the alt to describe the picture literally, which is a stricter rule than the criterion's equivalent-purpose test. The suggested patch, "Logotipo da linguagem de programação Python", would only add noise.
skeptic: The image is the site's template placeholder (images/comunidades-locais/default.png, a plain Python logo). It sits in the logo slot of the PythOnRio card, right under the h4 'PythOnRio'. The live page still has the same markup, and at least a dozen other cards (GruPy-MT, Py013, PyTche, Pug-CE...) use the same default.png with their own group name as alt. On this page the image works as a stand-in logo for the group, so naming the group serves the same purpose as the image. A screen reader user loses nothing that matters: the only visual content is a generic Python logo on a Python community site. SC 1.1.1 asks for an alternative that serves the equivalent purpose, not a literal description of the pixels, so 'describes something the image does not show' is a stricter rule than WCAG's. The suggested patch ('Logotipo da linguagem de programação Python') would add noise and fix nothing. A stronger argument would be that the placeholder is pure decoration and should have alt="" (F38). That is a different claim from this finding, and many auditors would treat it only as a redundancy advisory.

subject: GruPy-DF
message: The text alternative "GruPy-DF" repeats the image's file name: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.
ref: html > body > div > main > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(11) > img
auditor: This is the GruPy-DF group's logo in its card (src grupy-df.png). The crop and the full screenshot show a green stylised mark with the wordmark "grupy-df". The alt "GruPy-DF" is the group's name and the text in the logo, which is exactly the text alternative a logo needs. It matches the file name only because the file is named after the group. It is not an F30 file-name or placeholder alternative, and a screen reader user gets the same information a sighted user does. Repeating the h4 heading is redundant but does not fail 1.1.1. The rule had the right data (alt, src, image) and drew the wrong conclusion from a coincidence.
skeptic: This is the GruPy-DF group logo (grupy-df.png). The crop shows a green Python-themed shape with the visible wordmark 'grupy-df'. alt="GruPy-DF" gives the organisation name and the text in the logo, which is exactly the right alternative for a logo under the 1.1.1 Understanding document and G94. It is not a file name: there is no extension and the casing differs. The file is named after the group, not the other way round. F30 covers alternatives that are not alternatives, such as 'grupy-df.png' or 'image'. An alternative that happens to match the file stem while describing the image correctly is not an F30 case. The rule treats 'matches the file name' as a failure, which WCAG does not require. Repeating the card heading is redundant at most, not a 1.1.1 failure. The live page is unchanged.

message: The link text "2" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.
ref: #e-pagination > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
auditor: The element is the numbered pagination link "2" (href .../acessibilidade-digital/page/2/) in a standard pager shown as "1 2 Próxima página" below the article grid, where "1" is the current page and has aria-current="page". The snapshot and the live page agree (the live HTML is unchanged): the link sits in a list inside <nav aria-labelledby> whose accessible name is "Páginas de Acessibilidade digital". 2.4.4 accepts link text combined with programmatically determined link context, which includes the enclosing list and the labelled navigation landmark. In that context "2" clearly means page 2 of the Acessibilidade digital listing, and the destination's title, "Acessibilidade digital - Página 2 de 2", confirms it. The finding's claim that "nothing around it" gives the purpose is wrong: the nav name was in the context Rampa had (it appears in the packet's ancestors). Requiring the link text alone to state its purpose would be 2.4.9 (AAA), not 2.4.4. "Página 2" would be a nicer label, but its absence is not a 2.4.4 failure.
skeptic: The element is the "2" link in the archive's pagination: a <nav id="e-pagination" aria-labelledby="lbl-e-pagination"> named "Páginas de Acessibilidade digital" (an sr-only label placed right before the list), holding the list "1" (current page, a span), "2", "Próxima página". The live page still has the same markup. The finding says nothing around the link tells where it goes, and that is wrong: the link sits in a labelled pagination landmark, next to the current page "1" and a "Próxima página" link to the same URL. That context is programmatically determinable (the ancestor nav's accessible name, read out when a screen reader enters the landmark) and also visible, so a user can tell that "2" means page 2 of this listing. The destination, "Acessibilidade digital - Página 2 de 2", is what they would expect. Numbered links in a labelled pagination nav are the standard pattern that auditors accept under 2.4.4 (Level A, in context). Requiring "Página 2" in the link text itself is closer to the stricter 2.4.9 (link only). The checker had the nav name in its ancestors and still judged it wrongly, at low confidence.

auditor: The element is a 32px vehicle icon inside the 'Mais Acessados' link to service 2671. The link also shows the same text, 'Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)', and the live HTML is unchanged. An image inside a link may take an alt that states the link's function, so 1.1.1 does not require the alt to describe the picture. The alt only repeats the visible text. alt="" would be better practice (H2), but that redundancy is not a 1.1.1 failure. The suggested 'Ícone de veículo' would add nothing useful.
skeptic: The element is a 32x32 vehicle pictogram inside the 'Mais Acessados' link whose visible text is 'Emitir o licenciamento anual do veículo (CRLV)'. Its alt names the service the icon stands for, which is a functional or symbolic alternative, and WCAG 1.1.1 asks for equivalent purpose, not a description of how the icon looks. The alt repeats the adjacent link text. That is a redundancy issue (H2 or alt="" would be cleaner), but it is not a 1.1.1 failure, and it is not the mismatch the finding claims. The suggested patch, 'Ícone de veículo', would make it worse. The live markup is unchanged.

That makes it redundant, but redundancy is not a failure. The finding requires the alt to describe the icon's appearance ('Ícone de documento com cifrão'), which is a rule WCAG does not impose and would degrade the link name.

subject: Transferir a propriedade do veículo
message: The text alternative "Transferir a propriedade do veículo" describes something the image does not show.
ref: #cc-for-you > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(4) > a > div > img
auditor: The element is a vehicle icon inside the link to service 3284, next to the visible text 'Transferir a propriedade do veículo'. Its alt repeats the link text, so it states the link's function. That is an acceptable text alternative for an image inside a link. At worst the alt is redundant (alt="" per H2 would be cleaner), which is not a 1.1.1 failure. The patch's 'Ícone de veículo' would not improve the page.
skeptic: The same pattern as the other service icons. A vehicle pictogram sits in the link 'Transferir a propriedade do veículo', with the same text visible next to it. The alt conveys the meaning or function the icon represents rather than its look, which satisfies 1.1.1's equivalent purpose, and at worst it is redundant with the link text (a best-practice issue, alt="" preferred). The claim that the alt 'describes something the image does not show' applies an appearance-description rule that is stricter than, and different from, WCAG's.

subject: Ceará em Destaque
message: The text alternative "Ceará em Destaque" describes something the image does not show.
ref: #cc-for-you > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > img
auditor: The element is the featured photo of the 'Ceará em Destaque' bulletin card (a buggy on a sand dune). It is not inside a link, and the h3 directly above it is also 'Ceará em Destaque'. The alt names the publication, not what the photo shows, and the live HTML is the same. If the photo is treated as informative, the alt does not convey its content and the finding holds. If it is an illustration in a card whose information is all in the heading, date and link, it is decorative and the alt is only redundant. That would be at most an F38-style issue, not the inaccurate description the finding claims. Competent auditors would reasonably disagree about whether this photo carries information.
skeptic: The element is the featured photo of the 'Ceará em Destaque' bulletin card: a buggy on a dune with a beach behind it. It sits directly under the h3 'Ceará em Destaque' and above 'Boletim publicado! 09/10/2026 / Ler boletim'. The image is not a link, and its alt repeats the h3. Competent auditors would split three ways. One reading treats it as an informative photo, so the alt fails as claimed. Another treats it as ambience next to its own heading, in which case the right fix is alt="" (an F38-style issue) rather than a description. A third treats it as the edition's cover image, which is fairly identified by the publication's title. The evidence cannot settle which purpose the photo serves.

subject: Tarja-Especiais-Site-Interna-1

I checked for things that would excuse it: no aria-label or title on the link, no adjacent text, and the slide is not hidden. The live HTML still has this alt.

subject: Title

The browser's accessibility tree gives the link the name "Title" (from its contents); "Senado Federal" from the title attribute is only its description. skeptic: The header logo link (to www.senado.leg.br) holds only an img whose alt is "Title"; the image shows the text "SENADO FEDERAL". Chrome's AX tree gives the link the name "Title" (from contents), with the link's title attribute "Senado Federal" exposed only as a description. Rampa's own snapshot name "Senado Federal" is a naming error, but the claim stands. A placeholder alt like "Title" is not an equivalent for a functional logo image (F30). I found no technique that rescues it, and the live page is unchanged.

subject: Aumentar zoom

The live page's script shows that the button increases body zoom by 10% and the font size by 2px, so "Aumentar zoom" describes exactly what it does. subject: Selo comemorativo
message: The text alternative "Selo comemorativo" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: #body > header:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > a > img
auditor: The header's 60-years seal (an SVG reading '60 anos') is the only content of a link to https://60anos.unicamp.br/ (titled 'Home - Unicamp 60 Anos'), and it opens in a new tab. Its alt is 'Selo comemorativo', so the link is announced as 'Selo comemorativo'. That doesn't give the text in the image ('60 anos') or the link's purpose (the site for Unicamp's 60th anniversary), and nothing in the link's programmatic context supplies it. Under H30/F89, a functional image must give the link's purpose, so this is a real 1.1.1 failure (and a 2.4.4 one). The live page still has the same markup.
skeptic: The header seal image is the only content of a link to https://60anos.unicamp.br/ (opens the 60-years site in a new tab); the link has no aria-label or title, so its name is the alt "Selo comemorativo". The image visibly reads "60 anos", and the alt carries neither that text nor the destination, so a screen-reader user hears only 'commemorative seal' with no hint of the 60-years site. I looked for a reason it passes (a name on the link, a nearby text label, or an alt naming the anniversary) and found none on the live page. A functional image's alt must describe the link's purpose (H30), so this fails 1.1.1 as the finding says.

subject: Imagem do campus

subject: Placas de QR Code estão sendo afixadas nas árvores para proporcionar a pesquisadores e leigos uma observação mais apurada das plantas. Foto: Antonio Scarpinetti
message: The text alternative "Placas de QR Code estão sendo afixadas nas árvores para proporcionar a pesquisadores e leigos uma observação mais apurada das plantas. Foto: Antonio Scarpinetti" describes something the image does not show.
ref: #udum-secao-6acbfbfdda107 > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > img
auditor: This is the cover-block background behind the grid of eight navigation links (Ingresso, Graduação, etc.). So the text alternative states content the image doesn't show and is not an equivalent, which fails 1.1.1 as the finding says. skeptic: This is the background image of the cover block behind the eight navigation tiles (Ingresso, Graduação, ...). I downloaded the full 1920x660 photo: it shows a tree-lined campus path with students walking, and no QR code plates are visible. The alt is a reused news caption about QR plates being attached to trees, plus a photo credit, so it describes an event the image does not show. If the image is informative, the alt is not equivalent. If it is decorative, which it is here, it should be alt="", and a non-null misleading alt fails 1.1.1 too (F39). The suggested patch is wrong: it describes the HTML buttons, not the photo. That does not change the label.

subject: pesquisar
message: Nothing on screen tells what to enter in the field "pesquisar": its name is in aria-label, which only screen readers get.
ref: #gsc-i-id1
auditor: This is the Google CSE search box in the header, in a 'search-compressed' container. When collapsed, the input is transparent (opacity 0, per the theme CSS) and is drawn as a magnifying-glass icon (the CSS ::before on .gsib_a), which the screenshot shows at the field's position. Clicking it expands the field and shows the visible label 'Buscar no site'. The Understanding document for 3.3.2 explicitly accepts a magnifying-glass icon as the visible label of a search field, so the claim that nothing on screen says what to enter is wrong. The icon is a CSS pseudo-element and doesn't appear in the snapshot the model judged. Separately, the field doesn't expand on keyboard focus and its outline is removed, which raises a possible 2.4.7 issue, not 3.3.2.
skeptic: This is the Google CSE search input in the header, captured in its collapsed state: the input is transparent and a magnifying-glass icon (a CSS ::before on .gsib_a) shows where it is. The theme's all.min.js adds a <label for="gsc-i-id1">Buscar no site</label> after the input. When the box is clicked it gets .search-expand, and the CSS then displays that label as visible text above the field. The input also has title="pesquisar". So there is a visible text label when the field is in use, and the search icon labels it before then. The snapshot did not include either cue (the label is display:none in the collapsed state, and the icon is a pseudo-element), so 'nothing on screen tells what to enter' is not a fair reading of 3.3.2.

subject: img_senha
message: The text alternative "img_senha" is a file name or a placeholder.

auditor: Step illustration (a phone with a padlock and key) next to "Você preenche o formulário de dados pessoais e cria uma senha de acesso." skeptic: Phone with key and padlock, beside 'Você preenche o formulário de dados pessoais e cria uma senha de acesso.', with alt="img_senha". The live HTML confirms the alt and title are the file name and that no aria-hidden or presentation role applies, so screen readers announce 'img_senha'. That fails 1.1.1 whether the image is decorative (F39) or informative (F30). The patch's long description is a poor fix for a redundant illustration (alt="" would fit better), but the failure is real.

subject: INSCREVA-SE
message: The link text "INSCREVA-SE" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: #page-885654 > div > div:nth-of-type(9) > form > fieldset > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > a
auditor: This is the green 'INSCREVA-SE' button in the 'alertas grátis do Poder360' box. Its accessible name is just 'Inscreva-se', and it goes to the Poder360 WhatsApp channel. The blue button next to it has the same name and goes to Telegram (t.me/Poder360). I checked the snapshot and the live HTML, which has not changed: the link has no aria-label, aria-labelledby, title or hidden text. The only thing that tells it apart is the WhatsApp icon, a separate link (img alt 'WhatsApp') in a sibling div. The two only share a generic div wrapper, not a sentence, paragraph, list item, table cell or associated header. So the context is not programmatically determined in the sense of G53/H77/H78/H79/H81, and a user on this link (in a links list, or tabbing) hears only 'Inscreva-se' and has to move focus to find out which channel it is. Sighted users get that from the icon and the colour, but that does not satisfy 2.4.4. The message's 'nothing around this one tells it apart' overstates it a little, since the adjacent icon does, but the failure it describes is real. The suggested fix ('Inscreva-se no canal do WhatsApp') would resolve it.
skeptic: This is the green 'INSCREVA-SE' button (text 'Inscreva-se', uppercased by CSS) in the 'alertas grátis do Poder360' subscribe box. It links to the Poder360 WhatsApp channel. Its text is the same as the Telegram button's, which goes to t.me/Poder360. The only thing that tells it apart is the icon in the sibling div just before it: a separate <a> to the same URL whose img has alt "WhatsApp" (visible as the WhatsApp logo). I tried that as the reason it passes, and it does not hold. The icon and the button are in separate sibling divs (separate blocks), and the shared parent is a generic div. That is not the same sentence, paragraph, list item or table cell. The link has no aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby or title (the snapshot's ax data shows only name INSCREVA-SE), and the fieldset legend 'Formulário de cadastro' / label 'alertas grátis do Poder360' does not name the channel. Its first example is a 'Read More' link next to the content that explains it. The two links lead to different apps, so the channel is part of each link's purpose, and the purpose is not ambiguous to users in general. The message overstates the case ('nothing around this one'), since the logo sits right next to it visually and in the DOM. Read as a claim about programmatically determined link context, though, it is a real 2.4.4 failure. The live page (checked 2026-10-11) still has the same markup.

auditor: This is the department banner, a generic stock photo of open books (banner-departamento.png). The live HTML and CSS show that the white pill reading "Literatura Brasileira" is not part of the image: it is an HTML h2.titulo-sessao placed on top of it, and its bounds in the snapshot match the pill exactly. Because the image is decorative and the heading carries the meaning, alt="Banner padrão" also matches F39, where an image that should be ignored has a non-null alt. skeptic: The element is the category header image (banner-departamento.png, a generic stock photo of open books) with alt="Banner padrão", inside an <a> with no href. subject: unmarked|en|tarte Vaudoise à la creme

auditor: The h3 card headline 'Henry Harris' recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme' (Food section) has no lang markup, so the French dish name is read with English rules. 3.1.2 exempts proper names and words that have become part of the surrounding vernacular. 'Tarte vaudoise à la crème' is not English vernacular, and a strict auditor would ask for lang="fr" on the multi-word French phrase. Many others treat a dish's name in an English recipe headline as a name, which needs no language change, and the passage is short and still understandable. The evidence does not settle which reading applies; competent auditors would reasonably disagree.
skeptic: This is the h3 of a Food card, 'Dessert / Henry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme'. A regional dish name in an English recipe headline ('tarte Vaudoise', capitalised as a name; 'à la crème' close to the naturalised 'à la carte') can be read as a culinary name/term rather than a passage in French. The model asked for a description of the image's appearance (its patch: "Delivery truck icon"), which is not what 1.1.1 requires for a functional icon.

subject: YOUTUBE Marie Leloup plays Golden from "Kpop Demon Hunters" in the new Thomann Shop!
message: The link text "YOUTUBE Marie Leloup plays Golden from "Kpop Demon Hunters" in the new Thomann Shop!" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: #thomann-news > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > a:nth-of-type(1)
auditor: This is the first 'Thomann News' teaser card. It links to youtube.com/watch?v=7aDSIaFjkXM, and its name is 'YouTube Marie Leloup plays Golden from "Kpop Demon Hunters" in the new Thomann Shop!'. The third card has the same name apart from the casing of 'KPop' and links to Bx3MLITMdtM. Both cards are still on the live page. I checked both videos: each is on Thomann's own channel, has exactly that title and the same description. 7aDSIaFjkXM is a 31-second Short, and Bx3MLITMdtM is the 3:15 full video of the same performance. So the link text is the exact title of the video it opens and correctly describes where the link goes. The Understanding document for 2.4.4 says the name of the destination is enough to describe the link's purpose. It lists different text for links with different destinations only as a best practice. Both links deliver the content they advertise: Marie Leloup playing Golden in the Thomann shop, on YouTube. The ACT definition of 'equivalent resource' allows the destinations to contain different amounts of information. The finding treats 'different URL' as 'different purpose' and applies the best practice as a requirement, which is closer to 2.4.9 (AAA). This is a borderline call. The thumbnails differ visually (a vertical clip with blurred sides versus a 'VIOLIN COVER' title card), they are presentational (alt=""), and the proposed ACT rule fd3a94 could be read as failing an excerpt-versus-full pair. Even so, sighted users get no more information than screen-reader users about which card is the Short and which is the full video. Rampa never read the destinations.
skeptic: This is the first 'Thomann News' teaser card, a link to youtube.com/watch?v=7aDSIaFjkXM named 'YouTube Marie Leloup plays Golden from "Kpop Demon Hunters" in the new Thomann Shop!'. The third card (Bx3MLITMdtM) has the same name apart from letter case. The finding's facts are right: the names match, the URLs differ, and no programmatic context sets them apart. But Rampa never read the destinations. Both are Thomann Music videos with exactly these titles and the same description, showing the same performance: the first is a 31-second Short and the second the full 195-second video. Each link's text is the title of the video it opens, which Understanding 2.4.4 calls sufficient to describe a link's purpose. That document lists different text for different destinations only as a best practice. The ACT rule for 2.4.4 (fd3a94, still only proposed) passes links that lead to equivalent resources. Its definition says such resources may differ in how much information they hold, so long as the key content they advertise (this performance) is the same. A user can tell what either link does. The only thing the text does not reveal is which one is the short clip, and the visible text does not tell sighted users that either. Some auditors would still flag the duplicate as a 2.4.4 problem. The thumbnails' empty alt text is a separate question, not this claim. The live page still had both links on 2026-10-11.

subject: Entrar
message: The text "Entrar" has at most 3.42:1 contrast with what is behind it (#fefefe on #22a33e…#1e9f41), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a gradient). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
ref: #login-button-desktop
auditor: The element is the desktop 'Entrar' outline button in the header: white text on the header's green gradient. Sampling the screenshot inside the button gives #21a23e to #24a53a behind #fefefe, about 3.2:1 to 3.4:1. At 20px and weight 400 the text is not large, so it needs 4.5:1, and it fails. The page has an 'Alternar alto contraste' toggle, but G174 does not rescue this. G174 requires the alternate presentation to meet all other criteria, and that mode would keep failures such as the file-name alt on the 'Especiais' banner. So 1.4.3 fails in the default view.
skeptic: The measurement holds up. The 'Entrar' link in the header is #fefefe text on the green header gradient (about #20a13f behind it). style.css sets .btn-outline-cc to 1.25rem (20px) with font-weight 400 !important, so this is normal-size text needing 4.5:1, and it reaches only about 3.3-3.5:1 in the default presentation. The page, however, offers a visible, focusable 'Ativar alto contraste' toggle in the same header (its icon is about 3.8:1 against the green; it is also bound to Alt+Shift+C). Activating it sets body.contrast-active, and menu-mobile.css then forces the header to #111 with white text, which passes. This is technique G174. Whether that suffices is debatable: G174 needs the control itself to meet the contrast requirement, and it is an icon at 3.8:1, not text at 4.5:1. It also needs the alternate version to conform fully, which this page's other failures make doubtful. subject: compartilhe
message: The icon of this link ("compartilhe") has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #25d366). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
auditor: This is the WhatsApp share link in the left share bar: a white WhatsApp glyph on a #25d366 circle (class 'green'). The ratio 1.98:1 is measured correctly. However, #25d366 with a white glyph is WhatsApp's own brand logo presentation. The 1.4.11 Understanding document places logos under the 'essential' exception and says the exemption carries over normatively when the logo is used as a user interface component. Giving it more contrast is only a best practice there. The low contrast comes from the brand colors, not from a design choice by this site, so this is not a 1.4.11 failure as WCAG defines it. The rule applied G207 without the logo exception.
skeptic: WhatsApp share link (aria-label 'compartilhe'): a white WhatsApp glyph in a 24px circle with background #25d366 (live CSS .article-share ... a.green). White on #25d366 is 1.98:1 (recomputed), and the green circle against the white page is also 1.98:1, so the control's only visual has low contrast. However, the glyph is the WhatsApp brand logo in its official colorway, and the 1.4.11 Understanding exempts logos (the essential exception). It only advises a higher-contrast variant when a logo acts as a UI component, and is not exempt when the low contrast is the author's choice. Auditors reasonably split on social-media brand icons, so this is not settled.

subject: Próximo item
