subject: LabelText click,keydown
message: This element ("Busca IA do Tua Saúde") takes keyboard focus and listens to click, keydown, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as LabelText, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.
ref: #header > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > label
auditor: The header 'Busca IA do Tua Saúde' trigger is a <label for=headerSearch tabindex=0> with click and keydown listeners. The input it points to sits inside a hidden search container, so this label is the only way to open the search overlay. Chrome exposes it as LabelText with an empty computed name and no button or link role. Native labels do not respond to Enter, so the keyboard behavior is scripted. This is a scripted custom control whose role is not programmatically determinable (F59 pattern), so 4.1.2 fails. A <button> or role=button would fix it.
skeptic: Header '<label tabindex="0" for="headerSearch" class="search">Busca IA do Tua Saúde</label>'. The snapshot shows the real search form container (.header-tuasaude-search-container) hidden, so this focusable label, with click and keydown listeners, is the visible trigger that opens the AI search. Chrome exposes it as LabelText with no control role and an empty name of its own. A screen reader user who reaches it hears only text, not a button. Its native label behavior (focusing #headerSearch) cannot be what makes it work while that input is hidden. A scripted, focusable control with no role is the F59 pattern, so it fails 4.1.2 as reported.

subject: Logotipo Hous 360
message: The icon of this link ("Logotipo Hous 360") has at most 2.21:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#abaeb9 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
ref: #rodape > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > a
auditor: This is the footer credit link to Hous360, the site's developer. Its only visible content is an SVG of the Hous logotype, with fill #575d73 inside a group set to opacity="0.5", so it renders about #abaeb9 on white. I computed 2.21:1, so the measurement is right, and the crop shows a faint grey logo. Logos and logotypes fall under 1.4.11's essential exception, and the Understanding document says that exemption normatively carries over to a control whose only content is a logo. But the same document says a logo that normally has enough contrast loses the exemption when an author chooses to show it with low contrast. Here #575d73 at full opacity would be about 6.5:1, and the 50% fade is hard-coded in the theme, but I cannot tell whether it comes from Hous360's brand guidelines. Competent auditors would reasonably split on this. The finding also calls the logo an "icon" (G207), which understates the logo question.
skeptic: This is the footer "developed by" link to hous360.com.br. Its only visible content is an inline SVG logo whose paths are filled #575d73 inside <g opacity="0.5">. That renders exactly #abaeb9 on the white bar, about 2.2:1, matching the rule's measurement and the screenshot. The obvious defence is the logo exemption. However, the WCAG 2.2 Understanding for 1.4.11 says a logo presented at low contrast as an author choice, not because of brand colours, is not 'essential' and is not exempt. Here the brand colour #575d73 (about 6.5:1) is deliberately faded to 50% opacity, and no hover or focus style restores it (theme CSS checked). The logo is all that identifies the link, so it fails 1.4.11.

subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
ref: #rodape > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > a
auditor: This is the footer logo link to https://www.cultura.sp.gov.br/. Its only content is an image of the São Paulo state government crest ("Governo do Estado de São Paulo, Secretaria da Cultura"), which has alt="", and the link has no aria-label, title or other text. The accessibility tree shows a link with no name, and the live page has the same markup. A screen reader announces only "link", so the link fails 4.1.2 (and 2.4.4 and 1.1.1 by F89). The sibling logo links in that row have the same problem.
skeptic: This is a footer link to https://www.cultura.sp.gov.br/ whose only content is an image (the São Paulo government / Secretaria da Cultura crest) with alt="". There is no title, aria-label or text, and it is focusable and not hidden. The browser's accessibility tree gives the link no name, and the live HTML on 2026-10-11 is the same. This is documented failure F89 (also 2.4.4): screen readers announce just "link". The other logo links in the same row share the defect. Nearby text links do not name this link, so no passing technique applies.

subject: hidden image.png
message: This image is hidden from screen readers (alt=""), but it conveys what the text around it does not say: "Logo with the words 'METRÔ CONECTA'".
ref: #post-401 > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(4) > div:nth-of-type(1) > figure > img
auditor: The image (image.png, alt="") is the Metrô Conecta app icon with the words 'METRÔ CONECTA' beside it, shown next to 'Informe qualquer ocorrência em tempo real pelo nosso aplicativo.' and the App Store / Google Play badges. I searched the snapshot and the live HTML (unchanged): the app's name appears nowhere in text. The paragraph only says 'nosso aplicativo', and both store badge links also have alt="" images, so they have no names. The image of text is the only place the app is named, so marking it decorative hides information. That fails 1.1.1, as the finding says.
skeptic: The img (wp-image-13947, alt="") is the Metrô Conecta app logo: an icon plus the visible words "METRÔ CONECTA". I looked for a reason it could be decorative. The paragraph next to it says only "Informe qualquer ocorrência em tempo real pelo nosso aplicativo" ("our app") and never names the app. The App Store and Google Play badge links beside it also have alt="" images, so the name appears only in their hrefs, which users don't hear. The live page (checked 2026-10-11) still has the same markup. So the image is the only place the app's name is given. Logos are exempt from 1.4.5, not from 1.1.1, so hiding it from assistive technology fails 1.1.1 as the finding says.

I found no reason that makes it pass.

subject: Gaeilge
message: "Gaeilge" is in Irish, but it inherits the page's language (en): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="ga" to the link.
ref: html > body > header > div > div > div > div > nav > ul > li:nth-of-type(7) > a
auditor: The header navigation link 'Gaeilge' leads to the Irish-language site (index.ga.php). It is the name of the language written in Irish, and the live HTML has no lang attribute on it, so it inherits html lang="en". The Understanding document for 3.1.2 uses this exact case as its example ('Alternative language links': each language name, written in that language, carries a lang attribute). The language change is clearly intended, so the single-word and vernacular exceptions do not reasonably apply. This is a 3.1.2 failure.
skeptic: This is the header language-switcher link "Gaeilge" (to the Irish version). Neither the link nor any ancestor has a lang attribute, so it inherits lang="en"; the live page is the same. Marking language-switcher endonyms with lang is common practice, and here a change of language is clearly intended. But the Understanding document for 3.1.2 exempts proper names, and a language's name arguably is one. It also says single words should be treated as part of the surrounding language unless a change is clearly intended. And 'Gaeilge' is in everyday Hiberno-English use; the site's own English text uses Irish terms such as 'Gaeltacht' unmarked. Competent auditors split on single-word language-switcher links, so I cannot call this a clear failure.

subject: Alright!
message: The text "Alright!" has at most 1.69:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #13e47c), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a pseudo-element). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > button:nth-of-type(1) > span
auditor: The 'Alright!' text on the cookie banner's primary accept button is 18px bold, which is below the 18.66px bold large-text threshold, so it needs 4.5:1. The live CSS confirms '.cookie-consent-spice .consent-button--primary{background:#13e47c; color:#fff}' (the wrapper does have class cookie-consent-spice), which gives about 1.69:1. That fails even the 3:1 large-text threshold. The banner is shown on load, and the measurement matches the stylesheet. Real 1.4.3 failure.

The live stylesheet (vendor-fx.css) confirms the colours: `.cookie-consent-spice .consent-button--primary{background:#13e47c;color:var(--fx-color--neutral-white)}`. It is real text on an active control, so the incidental and logotype exceptions do not apply. The full-page screenshot does not show the banner, but the snapshot captured it and the live CSS confirms the colours.

subject: Español
message: "Español" is in Spanish, but it inherits the page's language (en-us): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="es" to the link.
ref: html > body > header:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a
auditor: This is the "Español" language-switcher link in the top official-notice banner, pointing to https://www.cdc.gov/spanish/. The snapshot shows <html lang="en-us"> and no lang attribute on the link or any of its ancestors, so the Spanish word is exposed as English. A language name in its own language is not a proper name or vernacular term under the 3.1.2 exceptions. The 3.1.2 Understanding document's own language-switcher example says each link's language is indicated with a lang attribute, and it shows Español marked with lang="es". The suggested fix (lang="es" on the link) is correct.
skeptic: This is the header link "Español" to the Spanish CDC site. The snapshot has exactly one lang attribute on the whole page, lang="en-us" on <html>. Neither the link nor any wrapper marks it as Spanish, and the live page shows the same markup. The Understanding document for 3.1.2 uses this exact case as its example: alternative-language links whose text is the language's name in that language need a lang attribute, and it shows "Español" with lang="es". None of the exceptions apply: the word is not a proper name, a technical term or English vernacular, and the change of language is clearly intended. The other "Español" links on the page have the same problem, but this finding names a real failure.

subject: Español
message: "Español" is in Spanish, but it inherits the page's language (en): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="es" to the link.
ref: #mplus-lang-toggle
auditor: The live markup is Español with no lang attribute, inside . 'Español' is a Spanish word, the name of the target language in a language switcher. It is not an English proper name or vernacular term, so English speech synthesis mispronounces it. Marking such language-selector items with their own language is the standard H58 practice, and auditors routinely report missing lang here under 3.1.2. The finding is correct.
skeptic: The "Español" link to the Spanish version has no lang attribute, in the snapshot or in the live HTML, so it inherits lang="en". The Understanding document for 3.1.2 uses exactly this case, "Alternative language links" (each language name in its own language, marked with lang), as its example. I checked whether it is a single word absorbed into English under the vernacular exception. It is not: a change of language is clearly intended for Spanish readers, and English rules would not pronounce the ñ correctly. None of the exceptions (proper name, technical term, indeterminate language, vernacular) applies cleanly.

subject: Accept
message: The text "Accept" has at most 4.13:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #d55140), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a background image). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

skeptic: The cookie banner's Accept button: white 15px bold text on the button's solid background. The site CSS sets .button-primary to background-color #d55140, and the screenshot pixels around the label are #d55140 (the banner is not dimmed). White on #d55140 is 4.13:1; 15px bold is not large text (needs 18.66px bold), so 4.5:1 applies. The background-image is only the small arrow sprite. Fails 1.4.3.

subject: hover: <a> "Fale com o Senado"; changed: color #ffffff → #cccccc, -webkit-text-fill-color #ffffff → #cccccc; #cccccc on #005b9e: 4.37:1 at best, 4.37:1 at worst · 16px, 400
message: When the pointer is over this control (hover), its text has a contrast of 4.37:1 at best with what is behind it, under the 4.5:1 WCAG 1.4.3 asks. Text must keep its contrast in every state a person puts it in; change the hover colors.
ref: #header-institucional > div:nth-of-type(1) > nav > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > a
auditor: The element is the 'Fale com o Senado' link in the dark blue global top bar (nav.navbar_global, background rgb(0,91,158) = #005b9e). I drove the live page in headless Edge at 1280x800 and hovered it. Its color changes from #ffffff to #cccccc (rule ':not(#_) .sf-wrapper .link-deep:hover { color: #ccc }' in essencial.css). Background, opacity, text-shadow and decoration stay the same. The text is 16px at weight 400, so it is not large text and needs 4.5:1. #cccccc on #005b9e works out to 4.37:1, which matches the probe. The rendered crop shows the same solid colors. WCAG 1.4.3 has no exemption for hover states: the hovered text is still text shown to the user, and in that state it falls below 4.5:1. The margin is small but it is a real failure.
skeptic: This is the 'Fale com o Senado' link in the dark blue top bar (16px, weight 400, so not large text). I hovered it on the live page in headless Edge at 1280x800 and waited past its 0.15s color transition. The text settles at #cccccc on the nav's solid #005b9e, with no background image, text-shadow or opacity change. That is 4.37:1 (I recomputed it), under 4.5:1, so it is not a mid-transition artefact. The 1.4.3 Understanding document puts text in hover and focus states in scope. I tried a G174 defence: the page has an 'Alto contraste' toggle, and in that mode this link is white on black. G174 only applies if the alternate presentation conforms, though, and the high-contrast mode has its own 1.4.3 failures: the phone number is #333 on black (1.66:1) and the 24px blue headings are #205c90 on black (2.99:1). So that defence fails and the finding stands. The live page matched the probe on 2026-10-11.

subject: hover: <a> "Sobre o Senado" (and 5 alike control(s)); changed: color #ffffff → #dddddd, -webkit-text-fill-color #ffffff → #dddddd; #dddddd on #007db8: 3.34:1 at best, 3.34:1 at worst · 16px, 400
message: When the pointer is over this control (hover), its text has a contrast of 3.34:1 at best with what is behind it, under the 4.5:1 WCAG 1.4.3 asks. Text must keep its contrast in every state a person puts it in; change the hover colors.
ref: #js-menu-0
auditor: The element is the 'Sobre o Senado' dropdown toggle (#js-menu-0) in the section menu bar (nav.navbar_control, background rgb(0,125,184) = #007db8). The same rule styles the other five toggles (js-menu-1 to js-menu-5). On the live page, hover changes the text color from #ffffff to #dddddd (rule ':not(#_) .sf-wrapper .link--nav:hover { color: #ddd }'), and the background stays #007db8. The text is 16px at weight 400, so it needs 4.5:1. #dddddd on #007db8 works out to 3.34:1, which matches the probe. Even the resting white text is only about 4.54:1 there. The hover-state text clearly fails 1.4.3. The probe's claim is accurate and the live page has not changed.
skeptic: This is the 'Sobre o Senado' dropdown toggle (#js-menu-0) in the section nav bar, one of six links that share the style. The text is 16px, weight 400. On the live page in headless Edge at 1280x800, hovering changes its color from #ffffff to #dddddd, the end value after the 0.15s transition. The background stays the nav's solid #007db8 (no image or shadow). That gives 3.34:1 (recomputed), well under 4.5:1. At rest, white on #007db8 is only 4.54:1, so hover pushes it below the threshold. Hover state text is in 1.4.3's scope per its Understanding document. The 'Alto contraste' toggle cannot rescue it under G174, because the high-contrast mode itself fails 1.4.3 elsewhere on the page (#333 on black at 1.66:1, 24px blue headings at 2.99:1). The live page matched the probe on 2026-10-11.

subject: Tab ×71 forward and Shift+Tab ×71 backward reached 70 element(s), never <button> "Próximo"; it is a native control that never took focus
message: The keyboard walk never reached this control with Tab or Shift+Tab: someone who uses a keyboard cannot operate it.
ref: #my-wrapper > main > section:nth-of-type(5) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > button
auditor: Próximo is the right-hand scroll button of the 'Novidades!' product carousel. Live at 1280x800 it is a plain native <button> (tabIndex 0, not disabled, not inert). Tabbing forward through the six product links scrolls the carousel to its end, and the site then sets display:none on the button's wrapper, so the forward walk skips it; a reverse walk on a page left in that scrolled state skips it too. On a fresh page, Shift+Tab from the first category link ('Musica') lands on Próximo, visible and operable. Its function is also available by keyboard anyway: every product in the carousel is Tab-reachable and scrolls into view on focus, and arrow keys scroll the container. So the functionality is keyboard operable and 2.1.1 is not failed; the probe's stateful walk measured the button only while it was hidden.
skeptic: The "Próximo" button scrolls the "Novidades" product strip. I checked the live page at 1280x800. It is a native button with no tabindex. Its wrapper turns display:none once the strip reaches its end, and Tabbing through the six product links scrolls the strip there. So a forward walk skips it, and a backward walk run in that same scrolled state skips it too. After a fresh load, Shift+Tab from below does reach it (7th Shift+Tab in my test), so the claim that Tab and Shift+Tab never reach it comes from the state the walk left the strip in. Its function, showing the next products, is also available by keyboard: every product link takes focus and scrolls the strip into view. So 2.1.1 is not failed.

subject: "d" changed what the window shows; each on two presses with focus on the body, and nothing changed in the same wait with no key
message: Pressing "d" with focus on the page, and no other key held, changes it: single character key shortcuts that work while no control has focus. Nothing on this page turns them off or remaps them. Let people turn them off, or remap them to include a key such as Ctrl or Alt, or make each work only while its control has focus (WCAG 2.1.4; F99). If a setting elsewhere, such as another page or the account settings, already does this, the criterion is satisfied: waive this finding (rampa waive).
ref: html > body
auditor: The claim is that pressing 'd' with focus on the body changes the page. Live at 1280x800 I pressed 'd' repeatedly, and also 'q', 'x', 'a' and no key at all, while logging DOM mutations and screenshot diffs. The only changes in every case came from the countdown digits and the header 'advantages' strip, which rotates on a fixed 3000 ms timer regardless of key presses (rotations at 2611, 5615, 8615, 11613, 14613 ms... with keys pressed in between and no extra change). The only document key listeners are analytics, Sentry and performance wrappers; there are no shortcut handlers. No single-character shortcut exists, so 2.1.4 does not apply. The probe attributed ambient animation to the key press.
skeptic: The finding is about single-key shortcuts on the body. On the live page, the only key listeners on window, document, html and body are keydown, keypress and keyup on document, all wrapped by the Sentry SDK. With focus on body, pressing "d" (and "x" and "j") changed nothing my checks caught: no scroll, no URL change, no focus move, and no DOM mutation other than the per-second countdown digits and the rotating header-advantages ticker. Those change just the same with no key pressed. The probe's 'changed what the window shows' most likely caught a timer tick, not a shortcut. No evidence of any character-key shortcut.

subject: Tab ×1: <a> "Chico Rei" focused and blurred; 0 px changed in the 135×76 px around the element, 0 px in the 1024000 px of the viewport (captured twice)

ref: #header-desktop-logo-wrapper > div > a
auditor: This is the 'Chico Rei' logo link in the desktop header, the first Tab stop. Live at 1280x800, Tab focuses it (:focus-visible matches) and its computed outline-style is none, with no box-shadow, border, background or underline change. Crops of the logo focused and unfocused are identical, and the only viewport changes come from the countdown timer. A keyboard user gets no visible focus indicator, so it fails 2.4.7.
skeptic: The desktop header logo link "Chico Rei" is the first Tab stop. On the live page at 1280x800, Tabbing to it gives :focus-visible but computed outline-style none, no box-shadow, and no background or decoration change. A crop with a 30 px margin is pixel-identical focused and blurred, which matches the probe's 0 px change. Other links on the page keep the browser's auto outline, so this rule specifically removes the indicator (F78). I found no other technique that makes focus visible here.

subject: Tab ×31 in a 390×844 window: <a> "Conheça nossas coleções!" at y 827; 25 of 25 grid points hit <div> "Mais desconto: 10% OFF nas compras a par" #contador (position: fixed, 390×170 px at y 674); painting it changed 0 px and hiding it 0 px; scroll-padding-bottom: 170px on html would keep focused elements clear of it
message: When this element receives keyboard focus, it is entirely hidden behind other content, so a keyboard user cannot see where focus is.
ref: #my-wrapper > main > section:nth-of-type(9) > p > a
auditor: This is the 'Conheça nossas coleções!' text link. Live at 390x844, Tab scrolls it to the bottom of the viewport (y≈827), and every hit-test point lands on the fixed #contador popup. The screenshot shows only the popup there, with the link fully covered. The #contador coupon/countdown popup is a non-modal, author-positioned fixed layer (390x170 px at the bottom of the 390x844 viewport, z-index 1000) that appears on load without user action. It does not close when focus leaves it and Escape does not dismiss it (checked live); its only close control is a 'Fechar' link earlier in the Tab order, so the user would have to move focus back to reveal the element. No scroll-padding is set. This is the sticky-footer pattern of F110. The focused link is entirely hidden by author content, so it fails 2.4.11.
skeptic: The link "Conheça nossas coleções!" in main is the subject. At 390x844 the #contador coupon banner is position:fixed, z-index 1000, 390x170 px at y 674, and the page sets no scroll-padding. html uses scroll-behavior:smooth, so I sampled the position over 1.5 s to rule out a mid-scroll capture. In two of my three live walks the link scrolled to mid-viewport and was visible. In the third, focused at Tab 31 as in Rampa's walk, it settled at y 827 and stayed fully under the banner. A sticky banner the author placed, not one the user opened, that entirely covers the focused element is failure F110. Whether it happens depends on the scroll state, but it is a real, reachable failure.

Live at 390x844, Tab brings it to y≈792, and all hit-test points land on the #contador popup, so it is fully covered. Every sampled point hits the fixed #contador banner (y 674-844), and with the banner hidden the link is visible. The banner is not user-opened, and the page has no scroll-padding (C43). subject: Tab ×43 in a 390×844 window: <a> "Central de ajuda" at y 619; 25 of 25 grid points hit <button> "SOBRE A CHICO REI" #footer-main-wrapper > div:nth-of-type(2) > button:nth-of-type(3) (position: static, 390×68 px at y 621); painting it changed 0 px and hiding it 0 px
message: When this element receives keyboard focus, it is entirely hidden behind other content, so a keyboard user cannot see where focus is.
ref: #footer-main-wrapper > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a:nth-of-type(1)
auditor: This is the 'Central de ajuda' link in the mobile footer accordion 'PRECISA DE AJUDA?', which is collapsed by default. Live at 390x844 the link stays in the Tab order while collapsed. Its container .collapsible-text has max-height:0 and overflow:hidden, so on focus the link is completely invisible: hit tests land on the neighbouring accordion buttons, and the screenshot shows no trace of it. Focus on invisible content is a real defect. But here it is hidden by clipping inside a collapsed panel, not overlapped by a sticky or overlay layer, which is the scenario 2.4.11's Understanding document describes. Many auditors would file this under 2.4.7 (no visible focus) and/or 2.4.3 instead. The probe's 'hidden behind the SOBRE A CHICO REI button' is a hit-test reading of that clipping. Whether 2.4.11 covers it is open to reasonable disagreement.

skeptic: This is the same VLibras hover panel. The strongest reason against the finding is that the barra CSS does include '.link-vlibras:hover' to keep the panel open, and with some pointer paths it does stay open. The finding names a real 1.4.13 failure, even though whether a given try fails depends on the pointer path.

auditor: 'Here's how you know' toggle (a role=button). The link is in the gov banner: 12px Poppins weight 300 text on white. subject: <a> "Managing Diabetes": link #006699 against text #444444, 1.56:1; no underline, border, weight, style, icon or pseudo-element sets it apart at rest
message: This link in a block of text is told apart from the text around it only by its color, and that color has a luminance contrast of 1.56:1 with the text, under 3:1 (F73). Underline it, or give it another cue that does not rely on color (WCAG 1.4.1; G183).
ref: #section51 > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
auditor: The link "Managing Diabetes" is the title at the start of a bullet in a MedlinePlus resource list ("Start Here"). Each bullet reads: title link, NIH icon, then the source organization in parentheses, with "Also in Spanish" on a second line. On the live page the title is #006699, 14px, regular weight, with no underline at rest (underline only on hover). The visible text next to it is not the li's #444444, which is what the rule compared against. It is span.orgs/desc-text in #666666 at 12px. The color contrast is under 3:1 either way (about 1.1:1 against the gray annotation), but color is not the only cue. The link is the item's title, set larger (14px against 12px) and in its own position, ahead of a smaller parenthetical attribution. That is the "visually evident from page design and context" case F73 sets apart from links inside prose, much like the titles of a list of search results. The finding says "only by its color", but it checked underline, border, weight, style and icon and ignored the font-size difference and the list layout. That applies F73/G183's inline-text-link test more strictly than SC 1.4.1 requires. The trailing "Spanish" link (12px, same size as "Also in") would be a stronger 1.4.1 case, but it is not this finding. This is borderline, and a strict auditor might still flag it.
skeptic: The 'Managing Diabetes' link is the title at the start of a bulleted resource-list item ("Start Here"); the item goes on with an NIH badge image, then the source organisation in parentheses (span.desc-text), then "Also in Spanish" on its own line. On the live page (headless Edge, 1280 px) the link is #006699 at 14px with no underline at rest (underline only on hover), but the text next to it is not #444444 at the same size, as the evidence implies: #444444 is the li color, which colors no visible text; the adjacent text is #666666 at 12px. So the link is set apart by a larger font size as well as by color, and is further separated by the badge image and the parentheses. That is exactly G182 example 3 (a list of article links with extra information, links not underlined but in a larger font than the rest), a sufficient technique for 1.4.1; F73 itself says links can be evident from page design and context, and this is a list-item title, not a link inside running text. The rule only counts underline, border, weight, style, icons and pseudo-elements, not font size, so it applied a stricter test than WCAG. (The "Spanish" link in "Also in Spanish" is a closer F73 case, but it is not the element reported here.)

The Understanding document for 1.4.11 (Figure 33, 'Text input focus style') rules this exact pattern a pass: a faint author outline (#CCC, 1.6:1) plus the visible caret, because the caret "does provide a sufficiently strong visual indication". Only a low-contrast custom caret fails (Figure 44), and that is not the case here. The probe measured only the ring and ignored the caret, so it applied a stricter test than 1.4.11 requires.
skeptic: The element is the "Search MedlinePlus" text input (#searchtext_primary). On focus it gets a Bootstrap-style #66afe9 border and a pale blue glow, with outline none. The probe is right that these are under 3:1 (the #66afe9 border is 2.37:1 on white; the glow is lighter). But this is a text input: when it gets focus it shows the native text caret, which keeps the default color (caret-color auto = #444444, 9.7:1 on the white field). The 1.4.11 Understanding document (Figure 33, "Text input focus style") passes exactly this case: a faint outline under 3:1 plus a visible caret, because the caret is a strong enough focus indication. It fails only when the caret is customised to low contrast (Figure 44), which is not so here. The probe compares screenshots, which normally hide the blinking caret, and then requires the styled ring to reach 3:1 by itself. That is stricter than what the criterion requires.

subject: focus: <a> "All events"; changed: background-color (control) #e8e6dc → #d4d0c3; #181710 on #7f7d75: 4.36:1 at best, 4.36:1 at worst · 16px, 500

ref: #content > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > a
auditor: The element is the 'All events' secondary button-link. I drove the live page (2026-10-11) with the cookie banner dismissed and focused it from the keyboard. In steady focus its text #28261b sits on #d4d0c3, which is 9.84:1. During the brief floating-focus flash it is still about 5.4:1. The probe's colours are those values seen through the cookie consent backdrop (#ccc-overlay, rgba(0,0,0,0.4)): #d4d0c3 x 0.6 = #7f7d75 and #28261b x 0.6 = #181710. skeptic: The element is the secondary 'All events' button link below the event cards. On the live page I tabbed onto it in headless Edge. Once focused it settles on a #d4d0c3 background with #28261b text, which is 9.84:1. It matches the anti-aliased pixels of the 2 px floating focus ring drawn 2 px outside the button (I sampled #7d7a77 there), so the probe took the ring, or a moment in the animation, as the text background. subject: Tab ×1: <button> "Close cookie control" focused and blurred; 240 px of its indicator around it: #5a5853 (240 px) next to #313147 (100%): 1.78:1
message: When this element has keyboard focus, its focus indicator (#5a5853, around it) has a contrast of 1.78:1 at most with the colors next to it, under the 3:1 that WCAG 1.4.11 asks of visual information needed to identify a state. Give the indicator a color with at least 3:1 against what surrounds it, such as an outline of 2 px that is dark on a light page.
ref: #ccc-close
auditor: The element is the 'Close cookie control' X button on the dark (#313147) cookie banner. The site uses the floating-focus library: on keyboard focus an author-styled div draws a 2px #5a5853 border (var(--color-text-tertiary)), 2px outside the button, and the native outline is suppressed (.floating-focused {outline-style:none}). I compared live screenshots before and after focus, after the helper flash had faded. The only change is 240 px of #5a5853 surrounded on both sides by #313147, which is 1.78:1. It is not a user-agent default indicator, it is the only thing that shows the focused state, and it is under the 3:1 that the 1.4.11 Understanding asks of focus indicators against adjacent colours.
skeptic: This is the 'Close cookie control' X button in the CIVIC cookie panel, a dark #313147 slide-out. After any keyboard use the site enables floating-focus-a11y, which removes the element's outline and draws a floating 2 px border in the outline colour, rgb(90,88,83) = #5a5853 (var(--color-text-tertiary)), 2 px outside the button. I confirmed on the live page that the floating element's border is solid 2px #5a5853 and that the button's computed outline-style is none. The ring has only panel colour on both sides, and #5a5853 against #313147 is 1.78:1. Once the transient overlay fades, nothing else marks focus. The UA-default exception does not apply because the author replaced the default ring; that default is only visible when the panel auto-focuses the button on load, before any key is pressed. This matches the Understanding 1.4.11 case of an external indicator that does not contrast with the adjacent background.

subject: boletim

The crop and the screenshot show a sheet with a folded corner, text lines and an 'A+' grade, which is a school report card. In Portuguese 'boletim' (as in 'boletim escolar') means report card, so the alt names exactly what the image shows. It is not a filename, a placeholder or a wrong description, so F30 does not apply. skeptic: The element is the 36x36 icon img (alt="boletim") inside the 'Boletim Escolar Digital' service link in the 'Serviços em destaque' carousel. The alt is redundant with the visible heading in the same link (alt="" per H2 would be cleaner), but an accurate, redundant alternative is not a 1.1.1 failure, and it is not what the finding claims. The crop was the right image, so the model misjudged with the context it had.

subject: Next
message: The icon of this button ("Next") has at most 1.61:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#cccccc on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
ref: #paragraph-d_p_carousel-500011 > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > button:nth-of-type(2)
auditor: The element is the slick 'Next' arrow button (40x40, aria-label 'Next', no visible text) of the partner-logo carousel (Transparência, MG App, 155 LigMinas, UAI...) near the foot of the page. In the screenshot it is a #cccccc disc with the chevron cut out to the white page, on a #ffffff background: 1.61:1. The chevron against the disc gives the same 1.61:1, so neither the glyph nor its shape reaches 3:1. The live site's CSS explains it: '.paragraph--type--d-p-carousel .field--name-field-d-p-cs-item-reference .slick-arrow::before{color:#000;font-size:2.5rem;opacity:.2}', and black at 20% on white is #cccccc. Hover only raises the opacity to .3 (#b3b3b3, about 2.1:1). The theme's focus rule (opacity 1) loses to that more specific selector, so focus does not help either. The glyph is the only visual information that identifies the control. The button is not disabled (no slick-disabled class) and its look is styled by the author, so no exception applies. It fails 1.4.11 (G207 not met), as the finding says.
skeptic: The element is slick's icon-only 'Next' arrow (40x40; its 'Next' text is font-size 0 and transparent) on the partner-logo carousel. Live CSS, fetched the same day as the run, draws it as a 40px fontello circle-chevron glyph via '.paragraph--type--d-p-carousel .field--name-field-d-p-cs-item-reference .slick-arrow::before{color:#000;opacity:.2}', which renders #cccccc. The screenshot confirms a #ccc disc with a white chevron cut-out on a white page, so both disc vs page and chevron vs disc are 1.61:1. Nothing that identifies the control reaches 3:1 (G207; the Understanding text covers any visual information needed to identify that a control is present). I looked for reasons it might pass and none held up. It is not inactive: the slick init has infinite:true and there is no slick-disabled or aria-disabled. It is author-styled, not a user-agent default. Hover only raises opacity to .3 (about 2.1:1), and the same specific rule overrides slick's :focus opacity:1. The page's contrast switcher (G174) does not help: every theme uses '.theme__X *', which never matches ::before, so the glyph stays #000 at 20%, which in the hivis theme means black on black. One nuance: the carousel autoplays (autoplay:true, every 3 s), and in the full-page screenshot the UAI logo's red text touches a 6px arc of the disc, so 'at most 1.61:1' is not literally true in every frame. That contact comes from moving slide content and does not make the control identifiable, and the chevron against the disc stays at 1.61:1 in every frame.

subject: Registre sua manifestação
message: The link text "Registre sua manifestação" is shared by 5 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: #main > div > section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > section > div > div > div > section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > h3 > a
auditor: This is the h3 link 'Registre sua manifestação' of the green Destaques card, which goes to the general Ouvidoria form (index.jsf). The next card has an h3 link and an icon link with the same name that go to index.jsf?canalAtendimento=D, which the live form shows as the 'Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher' channel. Sighted users tell the two cards apart only by their SVG icons ('Ouvidoria Nacional de Justiça' vs 'Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher'). Those icons are drawn as paths with no text alternative, and the icon links carry aria-label 'Registre sua manifestação'. So the two links have the same text and identical programmatic context (the h3 and the card), but their destinations are not equivalent. The ACT rule for 2.4.4 (fd3a94) counts identical names in identical contexts as a failure. The claim holds.
skeptic: This is the heading link 'Registre sua manifestação' of the second 'Destaques' card. That card's icon reads 'Ouvidoria Nacional de Justiça – Formulário Eletrônico' and the link goes to the general CNJ Ouvidoria form (index.jsf). The third card has identical heading and icon names but goes to index.jsf?canalAtendimento=D, which I confirmed opens the 'Ouvidoria Nacional da Mulher' form. The text that tells the cards apart exists only as SVG paths inside an aria-labelled sibling link, so nothing programmatic distinguishes this link, as claimed. But its own text accurately describes its destination, the page's general form, which the sidebar link with the same text also reaches. Understanding 2.4.4 calls distinct text for distinct destinations a best practice, and the under-described links are the women's-ombudsman ones. Competent auditors could fail this link as half of an indistinguishable pair or pass it.

subject: www.cnj.jus.br/comopeticionar.
message: The link text "www.cnj.jus.br/comopeticionar." is an address, not a purpose.

auditor: The link text is the URL 'www.cnj.jus.br/comopeticionar.' at the end of the sentence 'As demandas que sejam da competência do Plenário ou da Corregedoria Nacional de Justiça devem ser promovidas e encaminhadas de acordo com o Regimento Interno do CNJ, conforme orientações previstas na página …'. That enclosing sentence is programmatically determined context (G53), and it states the purpose: the page with guidance on filing such demands. The link does lead to 'Como acionar o CNJ', and the URL ('como peticionar', how to petition) is meaningful too. 2.4.4 does not forbid a URL as link text when the context gives the purpose, so this passes. The finding applies a stricter 'an address is not a purpose' rule.

subject: Início
message: The link text "Início" is shared by 4 links that lead to 4 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: #search-list > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
auditor: 'Início' (/inicio) is an entry of #search-list, the page-suggestion dropdown (ul.dropdown-menu) under the header search field. On the live page (checked the same day, markup unchanged) that list is display:none (Bootstrap .dropdown-menu rule in the theme's aui.css) until the user types two or more characters, and an inline script then shows only the entries whose name contains the query; Rampa's capture rendered the page without its theme stylesheet (default Times New Roman, the list about 59,000 px tall in the screenshot), so every entry looked like a visible link. The others are the home pages of other sites in the same list: /ppgci/incio, /df/inicio and /biomedicina-bacharelado-cb/inicio (the live list has 8 such entries). When the dropdown shows such entries together, nothing on the page, visual or programmatic, tells them apart for anyone (same text, same title attribute, no unit name), so their purpose is ambiguous to users in general and the 2.4.4 exception applies (Understanding 2.4.4; ACT rule fd3a94 background): different text for different destinations is a best practice, not a 2.4.4 requirement.
skeptic: The link 'Início' (href /inicio) is reported as sharing its text with links to other places. It is item 2 of ul#search-list, the search box's type-ahead suggestion dropdown (class dropdown-menu): on the live page aui.css hides it (.aui .dropdown-menu{display:none}) and the inline filter() script shows it only after two or more characters are typed, and then only the items whose name contains the query. Rampa captured the page with the theme CSS unapplied (the screenshot is unstyled HTML, even the sr-only skip links show), so 1,628 of its 3,302 items appeared as an always-visible list of links. The four 'Início' links in the snapshot go to /inicio (the UFPE home page), /ppgci/incio (302 to the PPGCI site), /df/inicio and /biomedicina-bacharelado-cb/inicio (302 to that course's site); I checked them on the live site, and the full list has eight. When the dropdown does show these items they look identical (same text, same chevron icon, no grouping or heading), so sighted users cannot tell them apart either. That is the 2.4.4 exception for purposes ambiguous to users in general: Understanding 2.4.4 says the person with a disability is not at a disadvantage when the page offers no context. ACT rule fd3a94 passes such pairs when there is no visual information that tells them apart, and it treats separate list items as different contexts. Different text for different destinations is only a best practice there.

'Imagem de alunos no Campus da PUC-Rio' is a generic but fair description of that: students outdoors in a campus-like setting. The picture cannot confirm the PUC-Rio location (the JPEG's EXIF credits peopleimages.com, so it is a stock photo), but a sighted visitor cannot see that either. The alternative still serves the equivalent purpose of this illustrative photo, so 1.1.1 is not failed. At most the photo could be treated as decorative and given alt="", which is a different point from the one reported.
skeptic: The element is the photo in the first slide of the top carousel (banner-bolsa-belkiss.jpg). It sits inside a link whose visible caption, real HTML text, reads 'Bolsa Belkiss e Carlos Infante de Castro'. I looked at the crop the model saw and at the full source file. auditor: The element is the Archdiocese's circular seal in the footer iframe. It is the only content of a link to https://arqrio.org.br (opens in a new tab) whose title is 'Site da Arquidiocese de São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro'; the live footer markup is the same. The browser computes the link's name from the alt, 'Selo da Arquidiocese de São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro', and exposes the title as its accessible description. That name identifies the organisation whose site the link opens: the destination's page title is 'Arquidiocese de São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro'. So it does convey where the link leads, which is what 1.1.1's clause for controls and technique H30 ask for. 'Site da' instead of 'Selo da' would be better practice, as in the WAI tutorial's 'W3C home'. But a linked logo whose alternative names the organisation it links to is not a 1.1.1 failure (nor a 2.4.4 one), so the finding applies a stricter rule than the criterion requires.
skeptic: The element is the Archdiocese seal in the footer iframe. It is the only content of a link to https://arqrio.org.br, and that link has the title 'Site da Arquidiocese de São Sebastião do Rio de Janeiro'. subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
ref: #google_ads_iframe_\/21715141650\,123935210\/metropoles\.com\/desktop_first_0 |> #bannerA > a:nth-of-type(1)
auditor: This is the image link (a.svg-anchor, data-asoch-targets ochImage) of a Google responsive display ad (Jeep Avenger) in the iframe 'Publicidade', inside an anchor container fixed to the bottom of the viewport. Its only content is an empty SVG painted with a CSS background image: no title, no aria-label, empty SVG hash, and the SVG is ignored in the accessibility tree. Chrome's accessibility tree lists the anchor as a focusable link with no name and no name source. An image as the only content of a link with no accessible name is the documented failure F89 of 4.1.2. The ad is third-party and rotates: the full-page screenshot does not show the fixed ad, and the live page may serve a different creative. At capture time, though, this unnamed link was on the page. Third-party status matters only for a conformance claim.
skeptic: This is the image link (data-asoch-targets 'ad0,ochImage') in the Google Jeep Avenger ad. The ad sits in a fixed bottom banner and is visible in the screenshot. subject: Image
message: The text alternative "Image" is a placeholder, not a description: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.
ref: #form1 > footer > img
auditor: The footer image cartoes.jpg sits under the address paragraph. The screenshot shows a strip of accepted payment methods (Visa, Mastercard, Elo, Amex, Diners, Aura, Hipercard, Discover, JCB, Hiper, Pix), and no nearby text lists them, so the image is informative. Chrome exposes it as an image named "Image" (name from alt), so a screen reader reads a placeholder that describes nothing (F30). If it were treated as decorative, a non-null alt like "Image" would still fail (F39). The live HTML still has alt="Image".
skeptic: The element is the footer image cartoes.jpg. The screenshot shows it rendered as a row of payment brand logos (Visa, Mastercard, Elo, Amex, Diners, Aura, Hipercard, Discover, JCB, Hiper, Pix), and no text on the page lists the accepted payment methods. Its alt is "Image", which is the same in the live HTML and is what the accessibility tree exposes as its name. Placeholder text like "image" is a documented 1.1.1 failure (F30). Even if the image were treated as decorative, a non-null alt such as "image" still fails (F39). The snapshot's null bounds and skipped image analysis are collector gaps that do not matter here, because the alt is in the DOM and the image is visibly rendered. No way for it to pass holds up.

subject: Nome
message: The field "Nome" asks for the user's full name but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="name" is missing.
ref: #wctnewsletter1_txtnome

It collects the subscriber's own name, a purpose on the WCAG Input Purposes list. Neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has an autocomplete attribute, and the ASP.NET name "wctnewsletter1$txtnome" is not a programmatic purpose. H98 is not met and the purpose cannot be determined, so the field fails 1.3.5. That would hold even if "given-name" were the better token than "name".
skeptic: This is the "Nome" field of the newsletter sign-up ("Receba nossas novidades e sugestões"), labelled only by its placeholder. It collects the subscriber's own name. Neither the snapshot (taken after scripts ran) nor the live HTML gives it an autocomplete attribute, and nothing else identifies its purpose. A name is a listed input purpose and HTML supports autocomplete, so the purpose is not programmatically determinable. Its validator accepts one or more words, so name (or given-name) would be the right token; either way the missing purpose is the real 1.3.5 failure the finding describes. I found no context or technique that makes it pass.

subject: Fale conosco pelo WhatsApp
message: The icon of this link ("Fale conosco pelo WhatsApp") has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #25d366). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
ref: #form1 > footer > div:nth-of-type(3) > a
auditor: This is the fixed floating link to wa.me: a 56px #25d366 disc holding the white FontAwesome WhatsApp glyph. The 1.98:1 figure is right, and the disc against the white page is also about 2:1. But the glyph is the WhatsApp logo shown in WhatsApp's own colors, the white mark on WhatsApp green of its app icon. Understanding 1.4.11 lists logos under the essential exception. It also says that when a logo is the only content of a control, the exemption "carries over" to that control normatively, and that a higher-contrast variant is only a recommended practice. The low contrast comes from the brand, not from an author dimming a logo that normally has good contrast. So this is not a 1.4.11 failure, and the G207 icon rule was applied to a brand logo. The control's focus indicator would still be in scope, but this finding is not about it.
skeptic: This is the floating WhatsApp link: the Font Awesome WhatsApp brand glyph, in white on a #25d366 circle. The screenshot confirms 1.98:1 between glyph and circle, so the measurement is right. But the icon is the WhatsApp logo in WhatsApp's own brand colours (#25D366 green with white), and WhatsApp's brand guidelines say not to modify the colours of its logos. The Understanding document for 1.4.11 exempts logos from contrast requirements. For logos that act as links or other controls, it calls a higher-contrast variant only a best practice. It denies the exemption only when the author lowers a logo's normal contrast, which is not the case here, since the WhatsApp mark's normal presentation has this contrast. So the claim that 1.4.11 requires 3:1 here applies a stricter rule than WCAG's documented interpretation. An auditor reading only the normative UI-component clause might still fail it, but the WCAG guidance supports a pass.

Without an href or tabindex it is probably not keyboard reachable either, but that is a separate 2.1.1 issue and does not affect this one.

subject: Digite aqui o que você procura

skeptic: The element is the header search field #txtBuscaProd. Its placeholder "Digite aqui o que você procura" is the only visible text on the field, which has no visible label. The site's own CSS sets .form-control{font-size:15px} and .form-control::placeholder{color:#aaa} (overriding Bootstrap's darker default), and the screenshot's glyph cores are exactly #aaaaaa on #ffffff, which is 2.32:1. The 1.4.3 Understanding document says the criterion applies to placeholder text. subject: Logo IC Cultural
message: The text alternative "Logo IC Cultural" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: #__next > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > picture > img
auditor: The element is the site logo in the header (it shows the mark and the word 'ItaúCultural'). It is the only content of a link to '/' and has alt 'Logo IC Cultural'. The live page is unchanged. When a linked site logo has a text alternative that names the organization, that is the usual, accepted pattern for a home link. Sighted users get the same cue: a logo that, by convention, leads home. So the alternative serves the equivalent purpose, and no documented 1.1.1 failure applies (not F30, F39 or F89). Adding 'página inicial', as in the WAI tutorial's 'W3C home', is best practice, not a 1.1.1 requirement. The alt has other flaws: the extra word 'Logo', and 'IC Cultural' where the logo reads 'Itaú Cultural'. The finding does not claim either one, and the alt still identifies the organization.
skeptic: The element is the header logo (a picture whose desktop source is the full \C ItaúCultural wordmark) and it is the only content of a link to "/". Its alt is "Logo IC Cultural", which becomes the link's whole accessible name. That matches the live page. The finding's factual claim holds: the name describes the image as a logo and never says "home". WAI's functional-images tutorial recommends "Example.com homepage" rather than "Example.com logo", and H30 says a link's only image should describe the link's function, so a strict auditor would fail it. The counter-argument is concrete, though. The alt names the organisation, a header logo linking to the site's home page is a universal convention, and a sighted user gets no more from the image than that, so the alt can be read as serving the equivalent purpose. WCAG's normative text and documented 1.1.1 failures (F30, F38, F65 and so on) do not cover this case. Competent auditors split on this exact pattern (many would call it best practice, or a 2.4.4 matter), so I cannot settle it either way.

subject: image banner
message: The text alternative "image banner" is too generic to describe the image.
ref: #__next > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > picture > img
patch_to: Banner da série Ocupação em vídeos com nomes de artistas brasileiros e botão 'Saber mais'.
auditor: The element is the 1280x450 banner image of the 'Ocupação em vídeos' promo. Its desktop source is ocupacaoConteudoDesk.png: a black field with a collage of the names of artists honored by the Ocupação series. subject: #__next > a
message: The icon of this link has at most 1.99:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #61ce70). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
ref: #__next > a
auditor: The element is the fixed floating link to wa.me: a 56 px circle in #61ce70 holding a white WhatsApp glyph, with no text. It also has no accessible name, which is a separate 4.1.2/2.4.4 issue. The measurement is right: the site CSS confirms white on #61ce70, which is 1.99:1. But the glyph is the WhatsApp brand logo, shown in the brand's own white-on-green presentation. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts logos under the essential exception. It also says the exemption normatively carries over to a control whose only visible content is the logo; using a higher-contrast variant is only a recommendation. The site's green is not WhatsApp's #25D366, but #25D366 with white gives the same 1.98:1. So the low contrast comes from the brand palette, not from an author choice that would void the exemption. This is a best-practice concern, not a 1.4.11 failure: the rule applied G207's icon test without the logo exception.
skeptic: The element is the fixed WhatsApp floating link. The CSS gives .floating-button a background of #61ce70, the SVG path has fill #fff, and the screenshot pixels confirm #ffffff on #61ce70, so the measured 1.99:1 is right. The graphic, though, is the WhatsApp brand logo: the speech bubble with a phone, white on green. Understanding 1.4.11 exempts logos and logotypes under the essential exception. It says that when a logo is the only visible content of a user interface component, the exemption normatively carries over to that component, and a higher-contrast variant is only a recommended practice. The author-choice caveat applies when a logo that normally has enough contrast is presented with less. That is not the case here: WhatsApp's approved pairings (white on #25D366, or green on white) measure 1.98:1, the same as this button, so the low contrast comes from the brand design, not from the site's slightly different green. The rule applied G207's icon requirement without the logo exception. The link does have a real problem, since it has no accessible name (2.4.4/4.1.2, F89), but that is a different criterion.

subject: Buscar
message: Nothing on screen tells what to enter in the field "Buscar": its label is on the page, but its text does not show: the label looks the same with its text made transparent.
ref: #searchDesk
auditor: The element is the desktop header search input (#searchDesk). At capture it sat in a collapsed form (width 0, overflow hidden, right -30%) past the 1280 px viewport edge, which is why the crop the model saw is blank. The site's live JS and CSS, which match the snapshot, show what happens when the user clicks the header magnifier icon. The form gets the class 'active' and widens to a 600 px white field, and the input takes focus. The field shows a 40 px magnifier icon at its left (a background image, bloom.svg) and a close X at its right. The 'Buscar' label is indeed hidden behind the input (z-index -1), and there is no placeholder. But Understanding 3.3.2 describes this exact case: a global search field in the header whose loupe icon serves as its visible label. It also says image labels meet the criterion. So the field has a label whenever it is shown. The checker never saw the field open. A keyboard user can tab into the hidden, collapsed input, but that is a focus-visibility issue (2.4.7), not a 3.3.2 failure.
skeptic: #searchDesk is the header search field. On desktop its form.accessibility-search is collapsed (width:0, right:-30%, overflow:hidden) and only opens to 600px with .active, when the user clicks the magnifier toggle in the header. When Rampa collected the page, the form, label and input all sat beyond the 1280px viewport (x 1302 to 1462). The crop the model saw is blank white, and the test that made the label text transparent compared pixels that were never on screen. In the open state the label is still hidden behind the input (position:absolute; z-index:-1). However, the input's CSS paints a magnifying-glass icon (bloom.svg) at its left edge, and the user reached the field through a magnifier button. Understanding 3.3.2 names exactly this case: a global header search field paired with a loupe icon, which serves as its visible label and needs no instructions. It also says images can serve as labels. So something on screen does tell the user what the field is for, and the claim that nothing does is an artefact of collecting the field while it was collapsed off-screen. The field is focusable while invisible, which is a focus-visibility concern (2.4.7), not 3.3.2.

subject: Home - Canada.ca
message: The page title "Home - Canada.ca" says nothing about this page.
ref: html
auditor: The finding is about the document title of the Canada.ca English home page. The title is "Home - Canada.ca" in the snapshot, and still was on the live page when I checked it on 2026-10-23. The page is the site's landing page. The screenshot shows the H1 "Canada.ca" with the tagline "The official website of the Government of Canada", then "Most requested" tasks, "Services and information" and "Your government". A title made of "Home" plus the site name states exactly that purpose. It also tells this page apart from the rest of the site, whose pages are titled "<topic> - Canada.ca" ("Jobs - Canada.ca", "Benefits - Canada.ca" and so on, in the destinations Rampa read). The only other destination with the same title is the basic-HTML version of this same page (?wbdisable=true). The title is not empty, placeholder text, a filename or a title shared by every page, so F25 does not apply, and it passes G88's checks (relevant to the content, identifies the page). The 2.4.2 Understanding document's own landing-page example is titled with the site's name. The page meets 2.4.2. Rampa had the title, URL, H1 and page content and judged wrongly that the title says nothing about the page, in effect asking a home page's title for more than the criterion requires.
skeptic: The finding is about the document title of the Canada.ca home page. The snapshot and the live page (fetched 2026-10-23, unchanged) both have the title "Home - Canada.ca". The page's h1 is "Canada.ca", its tagline is "The official website of the Government of Canada", and the page is the site's home portal to government services. So the title says exactly what the page is: the home page of the Canada.ca site. That meets 2.4.2. The checker had the title, the h1 and the page text, and still judged that the title says nothing about the page. That is a wrong judgment, and in effect it asks for more than WCAG requires.

The redundant heading link does not give this link a name, and the live page is unchanged. The claim holds.

The measured colours are exactly half of the real ones: Rampa sampled the pixels while the cookie-consent banner (uoe-consent, in a closed shadow root) laid its roughly 50% black backdrop over the viewport. In the screenshot's first viewport the white header reads #7f7f7f, and axe's 'could not decide' comes from that overlay. Content dimmed behind a temporary consent backdrop is not what 1.4.3 tests, and an auditor measures the page with the banner dismissed. Live CSS: the placeholder is #505050 on #ececec, about 6.83:1, which passes 4.5:1. The measured #282828 on #767676 is exactly half of that.
skeptic: The page was captured with the uoe-consent cookie banner open; its .uoe-backdrop is a fixed full-viewport #000 layer at opacity .5, and the measured colours are exactly half the real ones (the full-page screenshot shows the same areas undimmed below the first viewport). This is the same .form-control styling: placeholder #505050 on #ececec, 6.83:1, which passes 4.5:1. #282828 on #767676 is the backdrop-dimmed version.

subject: Pimoroni
message: The text alternative "Pimoroni" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: #navigation > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > svg
auditor: The element is the PIMORONI wordmark (svg role="img" aria-label="Pimoroni"), the only content of the header link to "/". The text alternative matches the wordmark word for word, and a logo that links to the site's home page is a convention users know, so "Pimoroni" gives screen reader users what sighted users get. The link also has title="Back to the home page", which Chrome exposes as its accessible description (the snapshot's CDP node has name "Pimoroni" and description "Back to the home page"), so the destination is available programmatically. Adding "home" to the alt is best practice from the WAI images tutorial, not a 1.1.1 requirement, and no documented failure covers a home logo link whose alt is the organisation's name. The live page has the same markup.
skeptic: The element is the PIMORONI wordmark SVG (role=img, aria-label="Pimoroni"). It is the only rendered content of the header logo link to "/", and on this page that link points back to the page itself. The text alternative matches the wordmark's text and names the site the link goes to. WCAG 1.1.1 does not require a linked logo's alternative to add "home": the WAI tutorial's "W3C home" is advisory, and no failure technique covers this. The link also has title="Back to the home page", which Chrome exposes as its accessible description (the snapshot's ax data shows it), so the destination is announced anyway. Requiring the alt text itself to state the destination is stricter than the criterion.

subject: Default Title
message: The text alternative "Default Title" is too generic to describe the image.
ref: #index > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > section:nth-of-type(1) > div > article:nth-of-type(1) > a > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
patch_to: Sonoff AirGuard E-Ink Zigbee Temperature and Humidity Sensor showing a digital reading.
auditor: This is the product photo of the Sonoff AirGuard e-ink sensor in the first 'Just landed' card. Its alt is "Default Title", Shopify's placeholder title for a product's only variant; the tile script on the live page still builds the alt from the variant title (alt="${hit.title}"). That text describes nothing in the image, and it is announced: the browser's accessible name for the card link is "Default Title New Sonoff AirGuard E-Ink Zigbee Temperature and Humidity Sensor". The photo could have been given alt="" because the product name sits next to it in the link, but a placeholder or programming reference used as the alternative is documented failure F30, so 1.1.1 fails as the finding says.
skeptic: This is the product photo in the first 'Just landed' card (the Sonoff AirGuard sensor). The snapshot shows alt="Default Title", and Chrome puts it into the card link's name ("Default Title New Sonoff AirGuard..."). That is Shopify's placeholder variant title: the live theme script still builds the alt from the variant title. It does not describe the photo, and it is not the empty alt that would let assistive technology skip an image that repeats the product name. Placeholder text used as a text alternative is the documented failure F30. I looked for a reason it could pass: it is not a collector artefact, and treating the image as decorative does not help, because the junk name is still announced. None held up.

subject: Default Title

It has alt="Default Title", which Chrome exposes as the image's name and as the start of the link's name ("Default Title New Sonoff Gen2 Zigbee Thermostatic Radiator Valve"). The text is Shopify's placeholder variant title, inserted by the theme's tile template. It neither describes the image nor lets assistive technology ignore it, which is failure F30 (placeholder text as a text alternative). No technique or context makes it pass.

subject: hidden svg
message: This image is hidden from screen readers (inside aria-hidden="true"), but it conveys what the text around it does not say: "Pimoroni logo and navigation menu with 'New', 'Popular', 'Treats!'".
ref: #header > div:nth-of-type(2) > svg
auditor: The element is the back layer of the header's seasonal Halloween scene (div.halloween-scene aria-hidden="true"): an svg.halloween-skyline whose only shape is a faint hill silhouette along the bottom of the header. It is pure decoration, so hiding it from assistive technology meets 1.1.1. The crop is the svg's bounding box, which covers the whole header, so it shows the real logo, search field and department links, which other elements draw and which are all exposed (the logo as an img named "Pimoroni", the departments as links). The 'logo and navigation menu' the finding credits to this image is that page content, not anything the image conveys.
skeptic: The element is the back-layer 'halloween-skyline' SVG inside div.halloween-scene aria-hidden="true". It sits at z-index -1 with pointer-events:none, and the page's own CSS describes it as a knocked-back scene of hills and a graveyard behind the header. The SVG holds one path and no text. Its crop is the whole 1280x158 header box, so it shows the logo, search box and department links painted over it, and the finding attributes those to the SVG. Those elements are exposed to assistive technology themselves (the logo link 'Pimoroni', the department navigation). This is pure decoration, and hiding it is what 1.1.1 asks.

subject: hidden svg
message: This image is hidden from screen readers (inside aria-hidden="true"), but it conveys what the text around it does not say: "Your cart is empty".
ref: #header > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > svg:nth-of-type(2)
auditor: The element is the front-layer svg.halloween-patch in the aria-hidden Halloween scene: silhouettes of a scarecrow and pumpkins at the right edge of the header. It is decoration and is correctly hidden. "Your cart is empty" is not in the image. It is the visible text and accessible name of the cart link (#cart_link), which lies inside the svg's bounding box, so the crop picked it up. Its crop includes the cart link drawn on top of it, and the finding credits that link's text "Your cart is empty" to the SVG. subject: Enter your e-mail address
message: The field "Enter your e-mail address" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.
ref: #mce-EMAIL
auditor: The element is the footer newsletter field (#mce-EMAIL, type="email", name="EMAIL"). The text beside it offers news 'delivered directly to your inbox', so it asks for the user's own address, which is information about the user, and 'email' is one of the listed input purposes. The field has no autocomplete attribute, both in the snapshot and on the live page today. type="email" gives only the data type, which the Understanding document says does not identify the purpose. Chrome's autofill check (FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError) flags the field too. Without autocomplete="email" (H98), 1.3.5 fails.
skeptic: The field is the footer newsletter input (type=email, id mce-EMAIL, placeholder "Enter your e-mail address"). It asks for the visitor's own e-mail address in order to subscribe them, so it collects information about the user. Neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has an autocomplete attribute on the input or its Mailchimp form. The Understanding document for 1.3.5 says type="email" does not identify whether the address is the user's own, and H98 (autocomplete="email") is the means of doing so. I found no technique that makes the field pass. I could not check the message's remark about Chromium's form check, but it does not change the verdict.

subject: Pimoroni
message: The link text "Pimoroni" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: #departments > nav > a:nth-of-type(3)
auditor: The element is the 'Pimoroni' link in the header's department navigation, between 'Pico' and 'Adafruit'. It leads to /collections/pimoroni, whose heading is 'Pimoroni' (Pimoroni's own products), so its text names its destination the same way its brand siblings do. The other link named "Pimoroni" is the logo, which leads home and carries the accessible description 'Back to the home page'; it is not in the department navigation. Understanding 2.4.4 calls different text for different destinations a best practice. ACT rule fd3a94 covers only links that share a programmatically determined context, which these two do not, and the general rule for identical names maps to 2.4.9 (AAA). 2.4.4 is met.
skeptic: The link 'Pimoroni' sits in the header's department navigation (Raspberry Pi, Pico, Pimoroni, Adafruit, Breakouts...) and goes to /collections/pimoroni. That page is titled 'Pimoroni Products' and its heading is 'Pimoroni'. The other link with the same name is the logo link to the home page, which also carries the description 'Back to the home page'. This link's text names its destination, just as its sibling brand link 'Adafruit' does, so its purpose can be determined. The Understanding document for 2.4.4 calls different text for different destinations a best practice, not a requirement, so the shared name alone is not a failure of 2.4.4.

subject: american-express
message: The text alternative "american-express" repeats the image's file name: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.
ref: #content > footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > picture > img
auditor: This is the American Express logo in the footer's row of accepted payment methods, with alt="american-express" (live page unchanged). The file name happens to be the brand name, so the alt text gives the same information the logo does: American Express is accepted. A screen reader reads it as "american express", and the neighbouring logos (visa, mastercard, paypal, klarna) work the same way. F30 covers text alternatives that are not alternatives, such as "image" or "spacer.gif", and this one is a real alternative. The rule flagged it only because the alt matches the file name, which is stricter than 1.1.1 requires.
skeptic: This is the American Express logo in the footer's row of accepted payment methods (the screenshot crop shows the blue AmEx mark). Its alt, "american-express", matches the file name american-express.png, but that name is itself an accurate alternative: it identifies the brand, as the sibling alts "visa", "mastercard", "paypal" and "klarna" do. F30 only covers file names that are not valid text alternatives in their own right ("Oct.jpg", "Chart.jpg"), and screen readers do not normally speak the hyphen. The rule treats any match with the file name as a failure, which is stricter than 1.1.1.

subject: Email address
message: The field "Email address" asks for the user's email address, but autocomplete="off" does not identify that purpose.
ref: #newsletter
auditor: This is the footer newsletter sign-up field (input#newsletter, type=email, with a visually hidden label "Email address"). It asks for the user's own email address, which is the 'email' purpose in the Input Purposes list, so 1.3.5 applies. It has autocomplete="off" in both the snapshot and the live page loaded in Edge, so no autocomplete token identifies its purpose. type="email" only describes the data format: it does not say whose email it is, and it is not the H98 technique. The purpose is therefore not programmatically identified, and this fails 1.3.5 as the finding says.
skeptic: This is the footer newsletter sign-up field (input type=email, id=newsletter, sr-only label "Email address", next to a "Sign up" button). It asks for the user's own email address, which is an Input Purpose (email), and it carries autocomplete="off". Nothing else on the field (no ARIA, no microdata) declares its purpose. The 1.3.5 Understanding document says type="email" does not establish that the field is the user's email, and that input purposes must still be programmatically determinable when authors turn autofill off. I found no technique that makes it pass, so the finding holds.

subject: Expand breadcrumb navigation
message: The icon of this button ("Expand breadcrumb navigation") has at most 2.65:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ff9718 on #666666). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
ref: #main > div:nth-of-type(1) > section > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > nav > button
auditor: This is the 40x40 'Expand breadcrumb navigation' button in the hero. It shows only an orange chevron icon and has no border or fill of its own. It sits inside the breadcrumb pill, whose computed background (live) is solid rgb(102,102,102). In the screenshot the chevron's pixels are #ff9718 and the surrounding pixels are uniform #666666, which gives 2.65:1. The live page computes the same colours. The chevron is the only visual cue that this control exists and what it does, so as an icon it needs 3:1 against adjacent colours under 1.4.11 (G207), and it falls short.
skeptic: This is the icon-only 'Expand breadcrumb navigation' toggle at the left of the breadcrumb pill over the hero image. I sampled the screenshot inside the button's 40x40 bounds: the chevron's solid pixels are #ff9718 and its surround is a uniform #666666, which gives 2.65:1, so the rule measured correctly. The button has no text and no boundary of its own (the pill's white outline wraps the whole breadcrumb, not the control), so the chevron is the only visual sign that the control exists and what it does. The 1.4.11 Understanding document treats such arrow symbols as graphical objects that need 3:1. I could not re-check the live page, which returned HTTP 403 to curl.

subject: searchbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a searchbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "searchbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
ref: #search-suggestions
auditor: This is the header search field (input#search-suggestions, type=search). It is tied to <label for="search-suggestions" class="sr-only"></label>, and that label is empty in both the snapshot and the live page. The CDP data in the snapshot shows the searchbox labelled by that label, with no name. I loaded the live page in headless Edge 155 and the searchbox's computed name is "". A minimal test in the same engine confirms that an empty associated label wins over the placeholder (the placeholder source is marked superseded). So in Chromium browsers the field has no accessible name, and the placeholder 'Search product or services' is exposed only as a placeholder. Some screen readers may still voice that placeholder and Firefox may use it as the name, but in the main engine the name cannot be programmatically determined, so the 4.1.2 claim holds.
skeptic: This is the header search input (type=search, placeholder "Search product or services"). It is associated with an sr-only <label for=search-suggestions> that is empty. The CDP tree in the snapshot gives it no name and no nameFrom, so in Chrome the finding is factually right. However, HTML-AAM 4.1.1 says that when the label yields nothing, the title and then the placeholder become the name. ACT rule e086e5 passes a placeholder-only field (Passed Example 5), and browsers expose the placeholder separately, where NVDA, JAWS, VoiceOver and TalkBack usually announce it, so users likely hear more than 'searchbox'. Under the spec the field has a name; in the dominant browser it does not. Competent auditors would reasonably split on whether that is a 4.1.2 failure. The empty label is plainly an authoring defect either way. I could not re-check the live page, which returned HTTP 403.

subject: Gray gradient
message: The text alternative "Gray gradient" names an image that is decorative.
ref: html > body > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > section > div:nth-of-type(2) > img:nth-of-type(2)
auditor: The element is a 32px gradient SVG (data-identity 'single-line-nav-fade-right') laid over the edge of the horizontally scrolling utility nav at the top of the header, a purely visual fade with no information. The snapshot's CDP tree exposes it as role image with name 'Gray gradient' from its alt, no role=presentation and no aria-hidden ancestor, and the live HTML still carries alt="Gray gradient". A decorative image that is not implemented so AT can ignore it fails 1.1.1 (documented failure F38: decorative img with non-null alt and no presentation role); screen readers announce 'Gray gradient, image' inside the nav. Should be alt="". This one sits at the right edge of the Locations list.
skeptic: A purely presentational fade overlay (data-identity='single-line-nav-fade-right', a 32x40 gray gradient SVG) at the edge of the header's utility bar; the screenshot shows it only softens the bar's edge and conveys no information. I looked for a reason it would pass: no aria-hidden or role=presentation on it or its ancestors, and the browser's accessibility tree exposes it as an image named 'Gray gradient' (nameFrom alt). The live page still has alt='Gray gradient'. A decorative image with a non-null alt that screen readers announce is documented failure F39 (and F38), so the claim holds.
