subject: Cleveland Clinic logo
message: The text alternative "Cleveland Clinic logo" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: html > body > header > div:nth-of-type(2) > a > div > img
auditor: The header logo image is the only content of the link to https://my.clevelandclinic.org/ (the home page); the link's computed name is 'Cleveland Clinic logo'. The alt identifies the organization, which is the conventional and widely accepted text alternative for a site logo linking home: users understand a banner logo link named for the site goes to its home page. 'Cleveland Clinic home' (without the word 'logo') would be better practice, but naming the site rather than literally saying 'home' is not a failure of 1.1.1 (nor of 2.4.4, given the banner context).
skeptic: The header logo is the only content of a link to the site home (https://my.clevelandclinic.org/), and the link's computed name is 'Cleveland Clinic logo'. The alt names the organisation, so it identifies the destination, and a site-name logo linking home is a convention users widely understand. 'Cleveland Clinic home' would be better practice, and the word 'logo' is redundant, but WCAG 1.1.1 (H30) only asks that the alt convey the link's purpose; no documented failure covers a logo alt that gives the site name. Treating this as a failure applies a stricter best-practice rule than the criterion.

subject: cancer icon
message: The text alternative "cancer icon" describes something the image does not show.
ref: #featured-services > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
auditor: The 38px icon above the 'Cancer' card heading in Featured Services is an awareness ribbon with a medical plus sign (file icon-ribbon-with-medical-cross), the standard cancer symbol. 'cancer icon' accurately conveys what it represents, so the claim that the alt describes something the image does not show is wrong. At most the icon is redundant with the adjacent h2 'Cancer' and could be alt="", but that is not the claim and redundant alt is not a 1.1.1 failure.
skeptic: The crop shows an awareness ribbon with a medical cross, the standard symbol for cancer, and it sits beside the 'Cancer' card heading. The alt 'cancer icon' gives the icon's meaning in context, which is what a text alternative should do. It does not describe something absent. The alt is at most redundant with the heading, which is not the failure claimed.

subject: primary care icon
message: The text alternative "primary care icon" describes something the image does not show.
ref: #featured-services > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(4) > div:nth-of-type(3) > img
auditor: The icon above the 'Primary Care' heading is an outlined medical cross (file icon-Primary-Care). It is not a mismatch; at most the icon is decorative and redundant with the heading, which is not what the finding claims.

A medical cross is a common symbol for general or primary care, and the alt names what the icon stands for in context. WCAG asks for text alternatives that serve the image's purpose, not a literal description, so this is not a mismatch. At worst it repeats the heading, which is not the failure claimed.

subject: Person sitting on a couch looking at their mobile phone.
message: The text alternative "Person sitting on a couch looking at their mobile phone." describes something the image does not show.
ref: #highlightPanelObject-2 > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
patch_to: A woman using her phone, surrounded by options for Emergency Care, Virtual Visits, Express Care, and Primary Care.
auditor: The large image in the 'Not Sure Where To Go for Care?' panel shows a woman sitting on a couch looking at her phone, with bubbles reading Emergency Care, Virtual Visits, Express Care and Primary Care. The alt 'Person sitting on a couch looking at their mobile phone.' describes exactly what the photo shows, so the claim is false. The bubble text is not in the alt, but the adjacent paragraph lists the same options (virtual visits, primary care, Express Care, the ER), so nothing essential is lost.
skeptic: The crop shows a woman sitting on a couch looking at her phone, with care-type bubbles around her. The alt describes exactly what the photo shows, so the claim is wrong. The bubble text (Emergency Care, Virtual Visits, Express Care, Primary Care) is left out of the alt, but the adjacent paragraph gives the same options, and that is not the failure reported.

subject: get care icon
message: The text alternative "get care icon" describes something the image does not show.
ref: #callsToActionObject-3 > article:nth-of-type(1) > img
auditor: The 60px icon above the 'Get Care' card heading is a check mark in a box inside a circle (file icon-appointments). Its alt 'get care icon' names what the icon stands for in that card; a text alternative may convey meaning rather than appearance, so this is not a mismatch failure. It is redundant with the h2 'Get Care' and alt="" would be cleaner, but that is a best-practice point, not the failure the finding claims.
skeptic: A decorative checkmark-in-a-box icon (asset icon-appointments) above the 'Get Care' heading of a call-to-action card. The alt 'get care icon' labels the icon by the section it illustrates, not by its look. That is a valid way to state an icon's purpose. It does not claim to show anything the image lacks. An empty alt would be cleaner because the heading repeats it, but redundancy is not the mismatch the finding reports.

message: The text alternative "." describes something the image does not show.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > header > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > img
auditor: The element is the 144px header icon (three pink-and-white blood cells on a navy disc) above 'About Cancer' and the H1 'Acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL)'. The snapshot and the live HTML (unchanged on 2026-10-23) both show with no aria-hidden or presentation role, so it is exposed as an image named '.' and screen readers announce something like 'dot, image' or 'graphic'. The icon is decorative because the H1 right below it gives the topic, so it should have a null alt (alt=""). A non-null placeholder alt on an image that should be ignored is documented failure F39. If the icon were treated as informative, '.' would not be an equivalent either. The message's wording ('describes something the image does not show') is loose, since '.' describes nothing. Read fairly, though, its claim is that the text alternative does not fit the image, and that is a real 1.1.1 failure.
skeptic: The element is the 144x144 header icon above the H1 (a navy circle with three white-and-magenta cells, file CRUK-Medical-icon-ALL-Myeloma-CLL), with alt="." and no aria-hidden, role=presentation or other hiding on it or its ancestors. The live page on 2026-10-23 still serves the same markup. I looked for a reason it could pass and found none. If the icon is decorative (likely, since it is a generic icon shared across blood cancer pages and adds nothing to the heading), WCAG needs a null alt so assistive technology can ignore it. A non-null "." keeps it exposed as an image named ".", which is failure F39 (and F38). If it is informative, "." is a placeholder that conveys nothing, which is failure F30. The message's wording ("describes something the image does not show") is loose, since "." describes nothing at all. Read fairly, though, its claim that "." is not a valid text alternative for this image is a real 1.1.1 failure either way.

subject: name@example.com
message: The label "name@example.com" does not say what to enter.
ref: #signup > div:nth-of-type(1) > input:nth-of-type(8)
auditor: This is the email field of the in-page 'Sign up to our emails' form (form aria-labelledby the heading). It has no <label> or aria-label, only placeholder="name@example.com" (the alt attribute is invalid on an input and is ignored), so the browser's accessible name is the placeholder. In context the visible and programmatic text clearly says what to enter: an example email address, next to the heading 'Sign up to our emails' and a 'Sign up' button. So 2.4.6 (labels describe purpose) is not failed. The real weakness is that the only label is a placeholder that disappears on input and is not a persistent label. That belongs under 3.3.2 (and arguably 1.3.1), not under 2.4.6 as the finding claims.
skeptic: This is the email input in the in-page newsletter form. It has no <label> or aria-label, gets its name from the placeholder "name@example.com", and has an invalid alt attribute. It sits inside a form labelled by the heading 'Sign up to our emails', next to a 'Sign up' button. 2.4.6 only requires that labels which exist describe the purpose. An example email address makes it unmistakable that an email address is wanted, especially in this context. The real weakness is a placeholder-only label that disappears on input and has no proper programmatic label, which belongs under 3.3.2 or 1.3.1/4.1.2. The claim that the text 'does not say what to enter' is not a 2.4.6 failure.

subject: name@example.com
message: The label "name@example.com" does not say what to enter.
ref: #signup-footer > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(1) > input:nth-of-type(8)
auditor: This is the footer newsletter email field. Its accessible name comes from aria-label="Enter your email address", which fully describes the purpose. The visible placeholder "name@example.com" also signals an email address, beside the 'Sign up to our emails' heading and a 'Sign up' button. The finding treats the placeholder as the label and calls it non-descriptive, but the label is descriptive, so this is not a 2.4.6 failure. The lack of a persistent visible label would at most be a 3.3.2 concern.
skeptic: This is the footer newsletter email input. It has aria-label="Enter your email address" (its computed accessible name in the snapshot) and the placeholder "name@example.com", under the visible heading 'Sign up to our emails' and next to a 'Sign up' button. The programmatic label says exactly what to enter. Even the visible placeholder identifies the expected input as an email address. The finding treats the placeholder as the only label and ignores the descriptive name, so there is no 2.4.6 failure.

subject: hidden .width-420_QM9bqBI.format-jpeg.jpg
message: This image is hidden from screen readers (alt=""), but it conveys what the text around it does not say: "The image contains the words 'URGENT!' and 'Rush' twice.".
ref: #content > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > figure > picture > img
auditor: The element is the page's lead (master) image: Michael Rothenstein's print Rush (1975), an airmail letter stamped URGENT over an airliner with 'Rush' written twice, shown in a figure whose figcaption reads 'Michael Rothenstein / Rush (1975) / Tate / (c) The estate of Michael Rothenstein', with the title linking to the artwork's own page. The live page (checked 2026-10-23) is unchanged: alt="" plus that caption. On a Contact page the image is a themed illustration for ambiance: it carries no information about contacting Tate, and the caption identifies the work for screen reader users. The words in it are part of the artwork's imagery, not text the page relies on, and 'Rush' is in fact the title the caption gives, so the finding's claim that the surrounding text does not say it is wrong. Requiring the words painted into an artwork to be transcribed goes beyond what 1.1.1 asks of an illustrative image identified by an adjacent caption. A short description in the alt would be good practice on an art museum site, but this is not a 1.1.1 failure.
skeptic: The element is the master image of the Contact us page: a reproduction of Michael Rothenstein's print 'Rush' (1975), an airmail envelope stamped URGENT over an airliner with 'Rush' written twice, marked alt="" inside a figure. Its visible figcaption, which is exposed to assistive technology, names the artist, the title 'Rush' (linked to the artwork's page on Tate's site), the date and the copyright, so the claim that the surrounding text does not say 'Rush' is false, and the model had this caption in its ancestor context. The 'URGENT!' stamp is a painted detail of the artwork, not information the contact page conveys. In context the picture is a thematic illustration, and the content needed to use the page is all in the text. A decorative image with null alt, identified by a caption, meets 1.1.1 (H67). Some auditors might still want a short alt describing the artwork, but the finding's claim, that words in the image carry information missing from the page, does not hold up. The live page on 2026-10-23 has the same markup.

subject: Image for Taboola Advertising Unit
message: The text alternative "Image for Taboola Advertising Unit" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: #internal_trc_9320554444 > div > a:nth-of-type(1) > div > span
patch_to: La Galerie: Apartamentos sofisticados com 4 suítes na Zona Sul de São Paulo
auditor: This is the first link of a Taboola sponsored card (La Galerie / Cyrela). The link is a.item-thumbnail-href: focusable, with no title and no aria-hidden. Its only content is span role=img aria-label='Image for Taboola Advertising Unit', so the snapshot's AX name for the link is that boilerplate. When an image is the only content of a link, its text alternative has to convey the link's purpose (H30, G94/G95). This generic label describes neither the picture nor the destination. The separate text link to the same href next to it does not repair this link: the two are not combined (H2), and an empty alt would leave an empty link (F89). The 1.1.1 failure is as reported; 2.4.4 is affected too.
skeptic: The element is a Taboola sponsored-content thumbnail (a span with role=img and aria-label 'Image for Taboola Advertising Unit') and is the only content of its own focusable link (a.item-thumbnail-href: no title, not aria-hidden, still in the tab order) to the La Galerie (Cyrela) landing page. The snapshot's accessibility name for that link is 'Image for Taboola Advertising Unit'. H30, a sufficient technique for 1.1.1, says that when an image is a link's only content, its alternative must describe the link's purpose. This generic label is placeholder text in the sense of F30: it says neither where the link goes nor what the picture shows (a rooftop terrace with lounge furniture over the São Paulo skyline). The text link next to it goes to the same URL and carries the ad title, but it is a separate tab stop, so it does not make this alternative serve the image link's purpose. Being third-party ad content does not change the result.

subject: WhatsApp
message: The icon of this link ("WhatsApp") has at most 1.98:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#25d366 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > nav > div > div > div:nth-of-type(3) > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
auditor: This is the header link 'WhatsApp' (aria-label WhatsApp). Its only content is the WhatsApp logo: a disc in WhatsApp's brand green #25D366 with a white glyph, shown with the other social logos in their own brand colours (screenshot). The measured contrast of about 1.98:1 is real. However, the Understanding document for 1.4.11 exempts logos under the essential exception ('the brand logo of an organization or product... is generally presented in the brand's specific colors; it is therefore exempt'). It also states that this exemption normatively carries over to a user interface component whose only visible content is the logo. The low contrast comes from WhatsApp's own brand colour, not from an author choice to dim a logo that normally contrasts, so the carve-out for author choice does not apply. Recommending a higher-contrast variant is a best practice; this is not a 1.4.11 failure.
skeptic: The element is the icon-only WhatsApp channel link in the site header. Its SVG ('whatsapp-negative' in the site sprite) is the WhatsApp mark drawn as a brand-green #25d366 disc with the glyph knocked out, on the white header, and the measured 1.98:1 is correct. However, the 1.4.11 Understanding document treats brand logos shown in the brand's own colours as exempt under the essential exception. For a logo that is the only visible content of a control, it only advises that authors 'may choose' a higher-contrast variant or 'should consider' adding an element; it does not require one. WhatsApp's own green is inherently about 2:1 on white, so this is not an author-chosen low-contrast presentation. Requiring 3:1 here is stricter than WCAG as its Understanding document reads.

The low contrast comes from WhatsApp's own green, not from an author's choice, so demanding 3:1 applies a stricter rule than WCAG's.

subject: WhatsApp
message: The icon of this link ("WhatsApp") has at most 1.94:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#65d072 on #ffffff). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
auditor: This is the footer link 'WhatsApp' (aria-label WhatsApp). Its only content is the outlined WhatsApp glyph in green (about #65D072 measured), in a row of outlined brand logos in their own colours: Facebook blue, Instagram, YouTube red, Threads (screenshot). It is the WhatsApp logo. 1.4.11's Understanding document exempts logos under the essential exception, and the exemption carries over to a control whose only content is the logo. The brand's normal green-on-white presentation is itself below 3:1, so this is not a case of a normally contrasting logo dimmed by author choice. This is not a 1.4.11 failure; a contrasting variant would be a best practice.
skeptic: The element is the icon-only WhatsApp link in the footer's social row. Its icon is the site's own outline redraw ('contoured-whatsapp' in the sprite, stroke hard-coded to #65D072), not the brand-green artwork. It measures 1.94:1 on white, and the screenshot confirms this. The 1.4.11 Understanding document exempts logos shown in their brand colours, but not low-contrast presentations that are the author's choice. It is unclear which applies here. This site-made outline in a near-brand green has essentially the contrast of WhatsApp's own green (1.98:1), which argues for the exemption. But its colour and style are the author's, which argues that it must meet 3:1. Competent auditors would split on this.

subject: SAIBA MAIS
message: The link text "SAIBA MAIS" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.
ref: #google_ads_iframe_\/1038086\/correiobraziliense\/interna\/politica\/in-image_0 |> #banner-nologo > a > div > div:nth-of-type(4)
patch_to: Saiba mais sobre os resultados das pesquisas
auditor: 'SAIBA MAIS' is a non-focusable div role=link nested inside the real anchor of the Google in-image ad. That anchor's accessible name is 'INFLEET Monitore por Vídeo SAIBA MAIS', and the whole ad goes to a single destination (infleet.com.br video telemetry). The advertiser name and headline sit in the same anchor, directly before the call to action, so the context is part of the very link users reach and activate, and that link's name describes its purpose. The claim that nothing around it tells where it goes is wrong, and the packet gave the model that ancestor link. Nesting role=link inside a link is a 4.1.2/1.3.1 coding problem, not a 2.4.4 failure.
skeptic: The element is the 'SAIBA MAIS' call-to-action inside a Google in-image ad iframe labelled 'Publicidade'. It is a non-focusable div with role=link, nested inside the ad's real anchor, whose accessible name is 'INFLEET Monitore por Vídeo SAIBA MAIS' and which leads to the same ad click-through. The advertiser and the offer ('INFLEET', 'Monitore por Vídeo') sit in that same enclosing link. So the CTA's purpose, learning more about INFLEET's video-monitoring offer, can be determined from directly associated context, and the packet showed that ancestor. The nested pseudo-links are a role or structure issue at most (4.1.2), not a 2.4.4 failure.

subject: LEIA MAIS
message: The link text "LEIA MAIS" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.
ref: #tbl-read-more-box-btn_Below\ Article\ Thumbnails\ \|\ Card\ 1_93205
auditor: 'Leia Mais' is Taboola's article expander, a[href=#] in div.tbl-read-more-box inside article#digital. The article is visibly clipped: it has class tbl-forkorts-article-active, and its box is 765px tall while the content is 3353px. The button sits at the cut-off in the screenshot. It does not navigate; it reveals the rest of the article. So 'does not tell where the link goes' misreads it, and sighted users get its purpose from the truncated text just above. Programmatically, though, its only context is the enclosing article, not a sentence, paragraph or list item. Screen reader users, for whom the text was never hidden, meet a bare 'Leia Mais' after the tags. Competent auditors would split between passing it (a single 'read more' within the article it expands) and failing 2.4.4. The clearer defect is 4.1.2: a link used as a disclosure button with no expanded state.
skeptic: The element is Taboola's 'Leia Mais' control: an a href="#" in div.tbl-read-more-box inside the article, which carries the class tbl-forkorts-article. The article is clipped to a short preview: its box ends near y=1441, while its text runs on for about 3,300 px. This button sits at the cut-off, just below the lead photo and caption, as the screenshot shows, and activating it expands the same article. It does not navigate anywhere. On a single-article page, placed inside the article at the end of its visible part, 'Leia mais' says what it does: read the rest of this article. The checker saw it only in DOM order, after the tags, as a link with an unknown destination. What remains, a link used as a button, belongs to 4.1.2, not 2.4.4.

subject: Capa
message: The link text "Capa" is shared by 3 links that lead to 3 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > header:nth-of-type(1) > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
auditor: This is the footer link 'Capa' in the Correio Braziliense column, href https://www.correiobraziliense.com.br/. Rampa read the destination: it is the site's home page. 'Capa' is the site's own word for its front page, so this link's text alone describes its purpose. Two other footer 'Capa' links do lead elsewhere: the Impresso one to impresso.correioweb.com.br and the Revista Encontro one to sites.correioweb.com.br/encontro/. That makes those links' text inadequate, not this one's. Understanding 2.4.4 lists different text for different destinations as a best practice, not a requirement. This one passes.
skeptic: The element is the first link ('Capa', title 'Capa') in the footer's Correio Braziliense column. That column is a list of the site's own sections, inside a header that also holds a 'Correio Braziliense' link to the same URL, and the link leads to the site's front page, as the destination title confirms. Two other 'Capa' links go to the print edition and to Revista Encontro. But on this site 'Capa' naturally means the site's own front page, which is exactly where this link goes, so its purpose can be determined from its text. Understanding 2.4.4 calls different text for different destinations a best practice, not a requirement. Any ambiguity lies in the other two 'Capa' links, not this one.

subject: Direito e Justiça
message: The link text "Direito e Justiça" is shared by 3 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > header:nth-of-type(1) > ul > li:nth-of-type(9) > a
auditor: This is the footer link 'Direito e Justiça' in the Correio Braziliense section list, href /direito-e-justica. Rampa read it: it is the 'Direito e Justiça' section page. The text names the destination exactly, and the side-menu link 'Direito e justiça' goes to the same page. The only differing one is the Impresso column's 'Direito e Justiça', which goes to the print-edition supplement. That is a problem with that link's text, not with this one. Identical text for different destinations is a best practice in Understanding 2.4.4, so this link does not fail 2.4.4.
skeptic: The element is 'Direito e Justiça' in the footer list of the site's sections. It goes to correiobraziliense.com.br/direito-e-justica, whose title and heading are 'Direito e Justiça', the same destination as the side-menu link with the same text. The link text names its destination exactly, so its purpose can be determined from the text alone. The third link with this text, under 'Impresso', goes to the print supplement. Understanding 2.4.4 treats distinct text for distinct destinations as a best practice, so this link does not fail because another one reuses its name.

subject: Capa
message: The link text "Capa" is shared by 3 links that lead to 3 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > ul:nth-of-type(2) > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
auditor: This is the footer link 'Capa' under the visual 'Impresso' label, href http://impresso.correioweb.com.br/, title 'Capa'. On the live page that address is the separate print-edition site, with stale content. On this site 'Capa' reads as the Correio Braziliense home page, which is where the first footer 'Capa' goes, and a third 'Capa' goes to Revista Encontro. The list item holds only the word. 'Impresso' is a separate link placed before the ul: it is styled like a heading but is not one, and it is outside the list item. So no programmatically determined link context sets this link apart; WCAG 2.2 defines that context as text in the same sentence, paragraph, list item or table cell. The 2.4.4 failure is as reported.
skeptic: The element is 'Capa' in the footer list under the 'Impresso' label. It goes to impresso.correioweb.com.br, the separate print-edition site (the live check shows a dated print front page), while two other 'Capa' links go to the site's home page and to Revista Encontro. Read on this site, 'Capa' suggests the site's own front page, so the text alone does not convey this destination. The only thing that tells it apart is the visual column label 'Impresso'. That label is a separate link placed before the list: it is not a heading (and H80 is only advisory anyway), and it is not in the same list item, sentence, paragraph or cell. The title attribute repeats 'Capa', and the other items in the list do not mention the print edition. No programmatically determined context gives the link's purpose, so the 2.4.4 claim holds.

subject: Direito e Justiça
message: The link text "Direito e Justiça" is shared by 3 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > ul:nth-of-type(2) > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
auditor: This is the footer link 'Direito e Justiça' under the visual 'Impresso' label, href impresso.correioweb.com.br/suplementos/direito-e-justica/capa_direitoejustica/. On the live page it redirects to the print edition's restricted-access page. The same text in the footer section list and in the side menu leads to the free web section /direito-e-justica. Only the visual 'Impresso' group label marks this one as the print-edition supplement, and that label is a separate link, not a heading, and not in the link's list item. Nothing in the link text or its programmatic context tells a user that this one leads to the print edition's subscriber area. The 2.4.4 failure is as reported.
skeptic: The element is 'Direito e Justiça' in the footer list under 'Impresso'. It goes to the print edition's Direito e Justiça supplement page on impresso.correioweb.com.br, which now meta-refreshes to a restricted-access page, while two other links with the same text go to the site's Direito e Justiça section. The 'Impresso' label is only a visual link placed before the list and is not programmatically associated, so nothing programmatic tells this link apart. Yet the text does name what the link leads to, the Direito & Justiça supplement, whose articles are also what the online section publishes. Auditors would split on whether 'print edition, behind restricted access' is part of the link's purpose that the text must convey, or a detail covered by the best-practice note on distinct text.

subject: Úlimas notícias
message: The link text "Úlimas notícias" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(4) > ul > li:nth-of-type(5) > a
auditor: This is the footer link 'Úlimas notícias' (sic) in the 'Imóvel' column, href //correiobraziliense.lugarcerto.com.br/noticias/noticias/, the real-estate portal's news. The Vrum column has an identical link to vrum.com.br/noticias/, and the site has its own 'Últimas Notícias' links. On a news site the text reads as that site's latest news. The real-estate destination is shown only by the 'Imóvel' column label, which is a separate link outside the list, not a heading, and not in the link's list item. Sibling items such as 'Ache seu imóvel' sit in other list items, which is not the link context WCAG 2.2 defines. The 2.4.4 failure is as reported.
skeptic: The element is 'Úlimas notícias' (sic) in the footer column of the Lugar Certo real-estate portal. It goes to correiobraziliense.lugarcerto.com.br/noticias/noticias/, while an identically worded link in the Vrum column goes to vrum.com.br/noticias/. On a news site, 'Últimas notícias' reads as the site's own latest news, so the text alone misleads. The only distinguishing context is the visual column label 'Imóvel' (a link in a separate header element, not a heading) and the sibling items about property. WCAG 2.1 and 2.2 cite the same list item, not the same list, as link context, and the Understanding asks for context directly associated with the link. The title attribute only repeats the text. The link's purpose cannot be determined programmatically, so the finding holds.

subject: Úlimas notícias
message: The link text "Úlimas notícias" is shared by 2 links that lead to 2 different places, and nothing around this one tells it apart.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(1) > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(5) > ul > li:nth-of-type(3) > a
auditor: This is the footer link 'Úlimas notícias' (sic) in the 'Vrum' column, href //www.vrum.com.br/noticias/, the vehicle portal's news. Its text is identical to the Lugar Certo column's link, which leads to a different external site. Only the visual 'Vrum' column label distinguishes it, and that label is a separate link before the list, not a heading, and not in the link's list item. Its list item and title attribute hold just 'Úlimas notícias', so neither the text nor programmatically determined context gives its purpose. The 2.4.4 failure is as reported.
skeptic: The element is 'Úlimas notícias' (sic) in the footer column of the Vrum vehicle portal. It goes to vrum.com.br/noticias/, while an identically worded link in the Imóvel column goes to the Lugar Certo real-estate news. On this news site, the text alone reads as the site's own latest news, which is not where it leads. What tells it apart is the visual 'Vrum' column label, a link in a separate header element and not a heading, and its sibling items about vehicles. Neither is in the same list item, sentence, paragraph or cell, which is the directly associated context that WCAG 2.2's definition and Understanding 2.4.4 describe. The title attribute repeats the text. Its purpose cannot be determined programmatically, so the 2.4.4 claim holds.

subject: Logo
message: The text alternative "Logo" is a file name or a placeholder.
ref: html > body > footer:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a > img
auditor: This is the visible desktop footer logo: an img with alt="Logo" that is the only content of a link to "/", so the link's computed name is "Logo". The image shows the brand wordmark "fleury" with the "100 anos" mark. "Logo" names the kind of image, not its content, in the same way as the "image" and "picture" examples in F30. It does not say whose logo it is or that the link goes to the home page, which 1.1.1 requires for a control. The header logo (alt "Fleury") and the hidden mobile footer (alt "Logo da Fleury") show the authors could do this properly. The live page still has alt="Logo" on this image.
skeptic: The element is the Fleury logo image (the word 'fleury' and the '100 anos' mark). It is the only content of the visible desktop footer's link to the home page (/). The link has no aria-label, title or hidden text, so its accessible name is just 'Logo' (snapshot: name from contents). I looked for a reason it could pass and found none. The image is functional, so it cannot be decorative. 'Logo' is neither the brand name nor the destination; it is a generic word of the same kind as F30's 'image' or 'picture'. Putting 'Logo' in place of the image loses both the information (Fleury) and the function (go to the home page), which is F30's test, so 1.1.1 fails. The finding's 'file name or a placeholder' holds on the placeholder side. The hidden mobile footer uses alt 'Logo da Fleury', which does not help the visible one, and the live page still serves alt='Logo' in this footer.

subject: App Store Badge
message: The text alternative "App Store Badge" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: html > body > footer:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > a:nth-of-type(2) > img
auditor: This is the App Store badge image (it reads "Baixar em App Store") that is the only content of a link to the Fleury Pacientes app on apps.apple.com. It sits next to the Google Play badge, under the visible text "Aplicativos Fleury". Its alt, "App Store Badge", does name the destination (the App Store) and tells it apart from the Google Play link. The image itself names no app, so the alternative carries about the same information and serves the same purpose. The extra word "Badge" and the missing "Baixar em" make the alt worse than "Baixar na App Store", but that is a wording problem, not a 1.1.1 failure. The claim that it does not say where the link leads does not hold, and the checker had the href and the surrounding text.
skeptic: The element is the 'Baixar em App Store' badge. It is the only content of a footer link to the Fleury Pacientes app on apps.apple.com, and it sits under the visible text 'Aplicativos Fleury'. The finding says its alt does not say where the link leads, but 'App Store Badge' does name the destination: the App Store. The image itself shows only 'Baixar em' and 'App Store', with no app name, so the alternative carries the image's essential information and its function (a link to the App Store). It could replace the image without loss, which is what 1.1.1 and F30's test ask. The extra word 'Badge', the dropped 'Baixar em' and the English wording on a pt-BR page are quality issues, not a 1.1.1 failure. Whether the link's purpose is clear without naming the app is a 2.4.4 question, not this criterion's ('Aplicativos Fleury' is a sibling paragraph, not a heading or the enclosing paragraph). The model had the alt, the crop and the href and misjudged them. The live page still has this alt.

subject: Política de Cookies
message: The text "Política de Cookies" has at most 4.31:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ed0f69 on #ffffff), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
ref: #onetrust-policy-text > a
auditor: This is the "Política de Cookies" link in the OneTrust cookie banner, which is visible when the page loads. The snapshot records its CSS colour as #ed0f69 on the banner's #ffffff background, at 13px bold. I sampled the screenshot pixels and the glyphs are #ed0f69 on pure white, which gives 4.31:1. 13px bold is well under the large-text threshold (14pt bold, about 18.7px), so 4.5:1 applies and the link fails. None of the exceptions (incidental text, logotype) apply. The live OneTrust configuration that GTM loads on www.fleury.com.br (domain script 0191d62a) still sets BannerLinksTextColor #ed0f69 on BackgroundColor #FFFFFF.
skeptic: The element is the 'Política de Cookies' link in the OneTrust cookie banner. It is 13px bold, which is normal-size text, so it needs 4.5:1. The snapshot took the colour #ed0f69 from CSS and found white behind the text. I measured the page screenshot myself: the solid core of the glyphs and of the underline is exactly #ed0f69 on #ffffff, which is 4.31:1. So the colour is not an anti-aliasing artefact or a banner caught fading in, and the dark overlay lies behind the banner, not over it. I looked for an exemption and found none: the link is active and visible, it is not a logotype, the Understanding document says brand colours are not exempt, and the page has no contrast switcher. The banner is third-party, but it is content on this page, in colours the site configured. It fails 1.4.3 as reported. I did not re-check the banner's styling on the live page.

subject: Digite aqui...
message: The placeholder "Digite aqui..." has a contrast of 3.74:1 with the field (#0a0a0a80 on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
ref: html > body > header:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > input
auditor: This is the desktop header search field. Its placeholder "Digite aqui..." is 16px regular text. The site's Tailwind v4 preflight sets ::placeholder to color-mix(currentcolor 50%, transparent), which over the field's white background gives about #848484. The screenshot pixels of the placeholder glyphs are #848484 on #ffffff, which is 3.74:1, below 4.5:1. The Understanding document for 1.4.3 says outright that the criterion covers placeholder text. The field is active, so the inactive-component exception does not apply. The live CSS is unchanged.
skeptic: The element is the header search field. Its only label is its placeholder 'Digite aqui...', at 16px regular weight. The site's Tailwind preflight sets ::placeholder to color-mix(in oklab, currentcolor 50%, transparent), and the field adds no placeholder colour of its own (I checked the live CSS). That gives rgba(10,10,10,0.5). The text pixels in the screenshot are #848484 on #ffffff, which is 3.74:1, below 4.5:1. The Understanding document for 1.4.3 says the criterion applies to placeholder text. The field is active, so no incidental-text exception applies, and I found no contrast switcher on the page. It fails 1.4.3 as reported, and the live page still has the same field and CSS.

subject: Alerta de Golpe
message: The text alternative "Alerta de Golpe" describes something the image does not show.
ref: html > body > section > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(4) > div > picture > img
patch_to: Alerta de segurança: Evite golpes. O Hcor não faz ligações para solicitar pagamentos antecipados.
auditor: The element is the active (not cloned) slide of the home-page Owl carousel: an unlinked banner image with alt "Alerta de Golpe" (scam alert). The crop Rampa used shows a banner whose own text reads "Alerta de segurança: Evite golpes.", with a warning icon and the sentence that Hcor does not phone to ask for advance payments for medicines, treatment changes or inpatient procedures. The alt names exactly what the image shows, so the claim that it describes something the image does not show is wrong. The alt is arguably incomplete, because it leaves out the warning sentence (the header's text bar "AVISO – GOLPE" gives a similar but not identical notice). That would be a different 1.1.1 claim, about the alt not carrying the same information, not the one reported. The live markup is unchanged.
skeptic: The element is the image on the 'Alerta de Golpe' hero carousel slide. It is the active owl-item, not a clone, and not inside a link. The crop the model saw shows a banner reading 'Alerta de segurança: Evite golpes.', an exclamation-mark bubble, and a warning that Hcor does not phone patients to ask for advance payments. The site header and the quick-access cards overlap the crop, but the banner is plainly visible. 'Alerta de Golpe' (scam alert) names exactly what the image shows, so the claim that the alternative describes something the image does not show is wrong. An auditor might separately find the alt too short for an image of text, since it leaves out the warning sentence (the page's top bar carries a similar warning as real text), but that is a different claim from the one reported.

subject: Banner FAQ - Portal do Paciente
message: The text alternative "Banner FAQ - Portal do Paciente" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: html > body > section > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(8) > div > a > picture > img
patch_to: Informações gerais para o atendimento no Portal do Paciente
auditor: The image is the only content of a carousel link to /imprensa/noticias/informacoes-gerais-para-o-atendimento-no-portal-do-paciente/, so the link's name is "Banner FAQ - Portal do Paciente". I opened that destination on the live site: its title is "FAQ - Hcor", its h1 is "FAQ", and every h2 is a question about the Portal do Paciente. The alt does say where the link leads (the Patient Portal FAQ). The leading word "Banner" is redundant, but it does not hide what the link does, so the functional-image part of 1.1.1 (H30: the alt gives the link's purpose) is met. Rampa never read the destination, which is the context that would have confirmed the match.
skeptic: The element is the image that is the only content of the 'Portal do Paciente' carousel slide link, so its alt 'Banner FAQ - Portal do Paciente' is the link's whole name, as the finding says. The link goes to /imprensa/noticias/informacoes-gerais-para-o-atendimento-no-portal-do-paciente/. I opened that page live, after the run: its title is 'FAQ - Hcor', its heading is 'FAQ', and it lists 15 questions about the Portal do Paciente and the Hcor app. So the alternative does say where the link leads, to an FAQ on the Patient Portal. The leading word 'Banner' is redundant but is not a 1.1.1 failure. Rampa never read the destination, so it could not see that the name matches it.

subject: Alerta de Golpe
message: The text alternative "Alerta de Golpe" describes something the image does not show.
ref: html > body > section > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(9) > div > picture > img
patch_to: Alerta de segurança: Evite golpes. O Hcor não faz ligações para solicitar pagamentos antecipados.
auditor: This is the same banner image with the same alt "Alerta de Golpe" as the active slide. It sits in an Owl Carousel "owl-item cloned" copy, which is not aria-hidden, so it is exposed, but it holds the same content. The crop shows "Alerta de segurança: Evite golpes." and the warning sentence, and "Alerta de Golpe" accurately names that subject, so the claim that the alt describes something the image does not show is wrong. If the alt fails 1.1.1 at all, it is because it leaves out the warning sentence, which is a different claim from the one reported.
skeptic: This is the copy of the 'Alerta de Golpe' scam-alert banner image that the carousel clones for looping (an owl-item marked cloned, not aria-hidden). It has the same alt as the original, and the model saw the same crop. The image shows 'Alerta de segurança: Evite golpes.' and a warning about scam calls, so 'Alerta de Golpe' describes what the image shows, and the mismatch the finding reports does not exist. A concern that the alt leaves out the banner's warning sentence would be a different claim, and the text warning bar at the top of the page partly covers it.

subject: Oncologia

F30 names file names that are not valid alternatives in their own right, ACT rule 9eb3f6 fails a file name with its extension even when the stem matches the subject, and F39 fails a non-null alt on an image that should be ignored, so the image fails whether it is informative or decorative. The image being off-screen at capture time (the widget is an infinite marquee) does not matter: it scrolls into view and screen readers read it anyway. I found no technique that makes it pass.

subject: logo-museu

subject: Digite seu Nome
message: The field "Digite seu Nome" asks for the user's full name but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="name" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.
ref: #dd-item-content-373
auditor: This is the footer newsletter sign-up's name field (type=text, name="name", placeholder 'Digite seu Nome', required). It collects the user's own name, a purpose in the WCAG input-purpose list, and HTML supports autocomplete, but the rendered input has no autocomplete attribute. The live page builds the field with the iSend forms script, whose text-field builder sets only type, id, name, placeholder, maxlength, class and required, so this is still true. The name attribute is not a programmatic purpose (H98 needs autocomplete), and the snapshot records Chromium's FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError for this input, which backs the message. 1.3.5 fails (autocomplete="name", or given-name, would be needed).
skeptic: This is the footer newsletter's 'Digite seu Nome' field, injected by the iSend widget: input type=text name=name, named only by its placeholder, with no autocomplete attribute and no form element around it. It asks for the visitor's own name, a purpose in the 1.3.5 list ('name'). The Understanding document says heuristics such as the name attribute are not enough: the purpose must be exposed through the autocomplete attribute (H98). The snapshot records Chromium's FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError issue on this field, which confirms the side claim. The live iSend script creates its inputs without ever setting autocomplete, so the field still fails today. Whether the right token is name or given-name, no purpose is identified.

subject: Masthead logo
message: The text alternative "Masthead logo" describes something the image does not show.
ref: #lazy_46231 > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
auditor: The element is the homepage masthead, an image of the words "THE IRISH TIMES" (I checked the crop and the screenshot). It is not in a link and is not hidden, and its alt is "Masthead logo". That alt names what kind of image it is but not what it says, so a screen reader user hears "Masthead logo" and never the publication's name. Strictly, the image does show a masthead logo, so the finding's wording ("describes something the image does not show") is a little off. The real defect is that the alt is generic and does not convey the logo's text (alt="The Irish Times" would). If the masthead were treated as decorative, a non-empty alt would instead fail F39. Either way 1.1.1 fails. The live page still has the same alt.
skeptic: The image is the page masthead, a wordmark reading "THE IRISH TIMES", with alt "Masthead logo". It is not inside a link, the page has no h1, and the small logo in the nav is aria-hidden, so this alt is how a screen reader user meets the publication name. The live page still uses it. The claim as worded, that the alt describes something the image does not show, does not hold: the image really is a masthead logo. The real 1.1.1 problem is different. The alt names the image type and leaves out the text the image shows (G94, close to F30), so it is not an equivalent. The element probably fails 1.1.1, but for a reason other than the one stated, and auditors could fairly split on whether the finding counts.

skeptic: The "LIVE UPDATES" kicker link above the lead story. It is a section link, so it is meaningful text. The snapshot records the CSS colour #979797, 12px, weight 400, on a plain white background. The darkest pixels of the label in the screenshot are #979797, so this is not an anti-aliasing artefact. The text is not large, not disabled, not decorative and not a logotype, so no exception applies, and the page offers no high-contrast alternative.

subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
ref: #lazy_45280 > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > a
auditor: This is the live-blog timeline entry link ("1 hour ago / The storm set to hit Ireland's west coast..."). The <a> wraps an <article> that holds the time and paragraph. In the snapshot, Chrome's accessibility tree gives the link role link and name "": Chromium does not take a name from the contents of an article descendant, and the link has no aria-label or title. So when a screen reader user tabs to this focusable link, or lists the links, it is announced only as "link", and its name is not programmatically determinable in the engine the page was tested in. That fails 4.1.2, and 2.4.4 as well. Some auditors might call this a browser quirk, since AccName 1.2 recursion would include the text. But the name the platform actually exposes is empty, and the fix is trivial. The live page has changed since the run: it no longer shows the live-blog lead, so I judged from the snapshot.
skeptic: The element is a live-blog entry link (a > article > time + p) whose visible text is "1 hour ago The storm set to hit...". The snapshot shows that Chrome's accessibility tree gives the link an empty name. This fits Chromium not taking a name from content through an <article> descendant, so the claim that the browser computes no name is accurate. Against counting it: <a><article> is valid HTML, and accname's recursive name-from-content step (2F/2H) would take the name from the text. So the empty name is a browser implementation choice, not missing author content. Name computations like axe-core's give the text, and browse-mode screen readers (NVDA, JAWS) read the link content anyway, so "announces only link" is overstated for them. Focus or API-based announcements in Chrome may still lose the name. Competent auditors would split on whether this is a 4.1.2 content failure or a user-agent quirk.

subject: fullepisode
message: The text alternative "fullepisode" describes something the image does not show.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > main > div > article > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > article > figure > a > img
patch_to: A hand holding a yellow tag labeled 'ELECTION SECURITY' with a play button icon.
auditor: The image is the thumbnail of the Oct 22 full-episode card (a still of a hand holding an 'Election Security' seal). It sits inside a link to the full-episode page together with a 'Watch' play label, so the link is announced as 'Watch fullepisode'. Next to it are the visible text 'Watch the Full Episode' and a title link 'PBS NewsHour from Oct 22, 2026' to the same page. This is a functional image in a link. Its alt only needs to convey the link's purpose, or could be empty because the text around it already does. 'fullepisode' is a sloppy string taken from the file name, but it says what the thumbnail stands for, and it does not describe anything the image is not. The still itself is illustrative, not information the user needs. Replacing the image with its alt loses no function or information, so this is not the 1.1.1 failure claimed; at most it is a quality issue. The live page still has the same markup.
skeptic: The image is the thumbnail inside the 'Watch' link of the 'Watch the Full Episode / PBS NewsHour from Oct 22, 2026' card. The link's accessible name is 'Watch fullepisode', and it leads to the October 22 full-episode page (title 'October 22, 2026 - PBS News Hour full episode'); the title link next to it has the same href. For an image inside a link, 1.1.1 asks the text alternative to convey the link's function, not to describe the photo (a hand holding an election-security seal). Together with 'Watch', 'fullepisode' names what the thumbnail stands for and where it leads. The alt is a run-together string taken from the file name and could be better (or empty, since the title link already covers it), but it is not false, so the claimed mismatch between alt and image is not a 1.1.1 failure. The live page is unchanged.

subject: Web ad - adjusted (1)
message: The text alternative "Web ad - adjusted (1)" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: #web-ad-image
patch_to: Join Press Pass: A new supporter program from PBS News
auditor: The image is a Press Pass promo banner, an image of text: 'Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass. A new supporter program from PBS News. Issue my Press Pass'. It is the only content of a link to /newshour/presspass/, and the link has no other name. Its alt 'Web ad - adjusted (1)' is the media-library or file name (Web-ad-adjusted-1.png), so the link is announced as 'Web ad - adjusted (1)'. That gives neither the banner's text nor where the link leads. This is a text alternative that is not an alternative (F30), and the H30 requirement that a link-only image describe the link's function is not met, so it is a real 1.1.1 failure; it also affects 2.4.4. The live page still has the same alt.
skeptic: The sidebar promo image is an image of text ('Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass. A new supporter program from PBS News. Issue my Press Pass'). It is the only content of a link to /newshour/presspass/ (title 'Press Pass | PBS News'). Its alt, and so the link's accessible name, is 'Web ad - adjusted (1)', a media-library file title. That is the F30 pattern, and it falls short of H30, which needs a linked image's alt to describe the link's function. Nothing else names the link: no aria-label, no title, and no nearby text. I found no technique that makes it pass. The live page still has this markup.

subject: Viewers Like You
message: The text alternative "Viewers Like You" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(4) > a > img
auditor: The image is the 'Viewers Like You' logo in the footer's 'Support for News Hour Provided By' list. The other logos in the list (BNSF Railway, Consumer Cellular, Raymond James) also use the funder's name as alt. This alt reproduces the logo's text exactly. The link redirects to pbs.org/donate/ (I checked this; Rampa had not read it), and a sighted user cannot tell that from the logo either, so screen-reader users get the same information as sighted users. 1.1.1 asks for a text alternative that serves the same purpose as the image, not one that states a destination the image itself does not show. Naming the destination ('donate') is advice from the WAI tutorial, and link purpose falls under 2.4.4, whose context and 'ambiguous to users in general' provisions apply here. The checker applied a stricter rule than 1.1.1 requires.
skeptic: The image is the 'VIEWERS LIKE YOU' funder logo in the footer list headed 'Support for News Hour Provided By', beside BNSF Railway, Consumer Cellular and Raymond James. Its link redirects to pbs.org/donate. The alt repeats the logo's text exactly, so it gives screen-reader users the same information the image gives sighted users and serves the same purpose (G94). Sighted users get no more destination information than 'Viewers Like You' in a funder credit either. 1.1.1 does not require an alt to state a destination the image itself does not show. Any doubt about where the link goes is shared by all users, which 2.4.4's exception for links ambiguous to users in general covers. The finding applies a stricter rule than the criterion.

subject: Enter your email address
message: The field "Enter your email address" asks for the user's email address, but autocomplete="off" does not identify that purpose.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > main > div > section > div:nth-of-type(5) > div > form > div:nth-of-type(1) > label > input:nth-of-type(7)
auditor: This is the visible sign-up field in the sidebar's 'Educate your inbox' box (input type=email name=email). It asks for the user's own email address to subscribe them to the politics newsletter, so it collects information about the user, and 'email' is one of the listed Input Purposes. The field has autocomplete="off" and no valid purpose token, so its purpose is not programmatically determinable. The 1.3.5 Understanding document says type="email" does not identify the purpose, and that purposes must stay determinable even when an author turns autofill off. H98 is not met, so this is a real 1.3.5 failure. The live HTML is unchanged.
skeptic: This is the sidebar 'Educate your inbox' newsletter field (input type=email name=email). Its only visible label is the placeholder, plus a visually hidden span. It collects the user's own email address, which is one of the listed input purposes. It has autocomplete='off' and no other purpose metadata. The 1.3.5 Understanding document says type=email does not make clear that the address is the user's own. It also says authors who turn autofill off must still make the purpose programmatically determinable; H98 would need autocomplete='email'. I found no reason it passes. The live page still has autocomplete='off'.

subject: Enter your email address
message: The placeholder "Enter your email address" has a contrast of 4.09:1 with the field (#757575 on #f0f1f8). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > main > div > section > div:nth-of-type(5) > div > form > div:nth-of-type(1) > label > input:nth-of-type(7)
auditor: The sidebar newsletter field shows the placeholder 'Enter your email address' as its only visible label; the label element's own text is visually hidden. The placeholder renders in the browser default #757575 at 13px, weight 400, on the field's background #f0f1f8 (the live CSS has .subscribe__box input {background-color:#f0f1f8; font-size:13px}). In the screenshot the darkest glyph pixels are #757575 on #f0f1f8, which is 4.09:1, below 4.5:1. skeptic: The placeholder 'Enter your email address' is the sidebar newsletter field's only visible label. The site's ::placeholder colour rules all target other forms (.subscribe__form, .popup, .subscribe-page__topper, .footer__subscribe-form), and none of them is an ancestor of this field, which sits in .sidebar__subscribe .subscribe__box. The site only sets the placeholder's opacity to 1, so Chromium's default placeholder colour, #757575, applies. The field's background is #f0f1f8 (.subscribe__box input). That works out to 4.09:1 at 13px and weight 400, below 4.5:1. The 1.4.3 Understanding document explicitly includes placeholder text. It is a real failure.

subject: hover: <a> "Política Quando os resultados da eleição serão anunciados e…" (and 2 alike control(s)); changed: color #0077b6 → #00cc99, -webkit-text-fill-color #0077b6 → #00cc99; #00cc99 on #ffffff: 2.08:1 at best, 2.08:1 at worst · 9.6px, 700
message: When the pointer is over this control (hover), its text has a contrast of 2.08:1 at best with what is behind it, under the 4.5:1 WCAG 1.4.3 asks. Text must keep its contrast in every state a person puts it in; change the hover colors.
ref: #digital > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(9) > div:nth-of-type(1) > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
auditor: This is the first link in the 'Saiba Mais' related-stories block. Its 'POLÍTICA' label is a strong element, 9.6 px and bold, coloured #0077b6 on white. On the live page, hovering the link applies the rule '.read-more ul li a:hover { color: rgb(0,204,153) }', so the label turns #00cc99 on white, about 2.08:1. That is small text, so it needs 4.5:1. The headline span keeps #333. The Understanding document for 1.4.3 says the criterion covers text shown while the pointer hovers, so the hover state fails as reported. The two other links in the block share the same rule.
skeptic: This is a 'Saiba Mais' related-article link. Its category label 'POLÍTICA' is a strong element at 9.6 px, bold and uppercase, and inherits the link colour. I checked live: the rule '.read-more ul li a:hover { color: #00cc99 }' turns the label from #0077b6 (about 4.9:1) to #00cc99 on the white card, which is 2.08:1 (I recomputed it). It is small text, so it needs 4.5:1. The 1.4.3 Understanding says text shown while hovered must also have sufficient contrast. I found no exemption: the label is not incidental or a logo, and nothing changes behind it on hover. The title span stays #333 and passes, so the failure is the label, which is what the evidence measures.

subject: before: whole; with the spacing: 22 px cut down by <div> #digital > div:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(9) > div:nth-of-type(1)

On the live page, with the 1.4.12 values applied (line-height 1.5, letter-spacing 0.12em, word-spacing 0.16em, 2em after paragraphs), the card grows: the container's scrollHeight becomes 306 against a clientHeight of 280, and the span's last line falls about 26 px below the clip. In my screenshot the headline ends at '...anunciados e como' and 'acompanhá-los?' is no longer visible. Visible content is lost, which is failure F104, as reported.
skeptic: This is the title span of a 'Saiba Mais' card ('Quando os resultados da eleição serão anunciados e como acompanhá-los?'). I reproduced it live at 1280x1024: the cards sit in div.slick-slider, which has a fixed height of 280px and overflow hidden. The span has line-height 16px (1.0). With the WCAG 1.4.12 spacing values, the title grows from 3 lines (49 px) to 4 lines (97 px), and the slider clips the bottom line. In the screenshot the last words, 'acompanhá-los?', disappear. The text was whole before the change. This is loss of content under the spacing values the criterion requires, and nothing in the page lets the user see the clipped line. I found no artefact.

auditor: The 'FoundationOne®...' sidebar link at 390x844, reported as entirely hidden behind the OneTrust cookie banner. The probe's own record shows a race on load. The walk began about 3.9 s after load, before the banner appeared. At Tab 9 the banner was still sliding in: the recorded banner y of 548 is mid-animation, and its resting y is 452. The banner then slides over it for under a second, after which OneTrust moves focus onto the banner. With the banner showing, Tab, Shift+Tab and ArrowDown then Tab all keep focus inside the banner, behind a dark page filter, and Escape closes it. Per the 2.4.11 Understanding, making the banner modal so the user must dismiss it before navigating the page is a way to pass. A keyboard user is never left with focus on a hidden page element: the moment caught here is a brief animation race, after which focus goes to visible banner controls. skeptic: FoundationOne link in the sidebar; the finding says that at 390x844 it is fully hidden behind the OneTrust cookie banner when focused. The snapshot's own walk record shows that this walk did not wait for idle (idleMs 0). It reached the link at Tab x9, about 4.35 s after load and 35 to 100 ms per key. One step later, focus was inside the banner and stayed trapped there. I drove the live page in headless Edge at 390x844. The banner comes with a full-viewport 50% black overlay that blocks the page. About 0.8 s after it appears it takes focus. After that, Tab, Shift+Tab and ArrowDown then Tab all cycle inside its four controls, and Escape dismisses it. In its settled state the banner is effectively modal, which the Understanding for 2.4.11 lists as a way to pass ('making the banner modal so the user has to dismiss the banner before navigating through the page'). A keyboard user cannot move focus to the link while the banner is up, and once it is dismissed nothing covers the link. The probe caught a transient state during load, before the banner took focus, so the claim does not hold for the page as users meet it. The page may have changed since the run, but the snapshot's own trap record shows the same banner trap then.

Give the indicator a color with at least 3:1 against what surrounds it, such as an outline of 2 px that is dark on a light page.
ref: html > body > footer > section:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > nav > ul > li:nth-of-type(2) > a
auditor: This is a footer social icon link. The site removes its outline, and the focus cue is only '.footer .social a:focus {transform: scale(1.1)}', so the LinkedIn #0077b5 tile grows by about 2 px a side on the #194f7f footer. I confirmed that on the live page with crops of the focused and blurred states. The growing edge has about 1.75:1 against the footer, and the glyph's own growth is about 1 px. The focus indicator does not reach 3:1 against the adjacent colour, so it fails 1.4.11 (F78), as reported.
skeptic: Footer LinkedIn icon link (#0077b5 square, white glyph, on #194f7f). On the live page, focus only applies transform: scale(1.1). The band of icon colour against the footer measures 1.75:1, as the probe says. The white glyph, also enlarged, contrasts about 4.8:1 with the fill, and 1.4.11 does not compare the focused and unfocused states. Whether this scale-only indicator fails 1.4.11 is open to reasonable disagreement.

subject: "I" changed what the window shows; each on two presses with focus on the body, and nothing changed in the same wait with no key
message: Pressing "I" with focus on the page, and no other key held, changes it: single character key shortcuts that work while no control has focus. Nothing on this page turns them off or remaps them. Let people turn them off, or remap them to include a key such as Ctrl or Alt, or make each work only while its control has focus (WCAG 2.1.4; F99). If a setting elsewhere, such as another page or the account settings, already does this, the criterion is satisfied: waive this finding (rampa waive).
ref: html > body
auditor: The claim is that pressing 'I' with focus on the body changes the page. I listed the live page's key listeners over CDP: there are only Bootstrap's delegated dropdown keydown/keyup handlers and a jQuery body keyup that reacts to Esc (keyCode 27). Nothing handles 'I'. In repeated trials, screen changes came at random with 'I', 'i', Shift+I and other letters alike. They match the hero carousel's autoplay (the region 13,151 to 1267,714) and the animated WhatsApp popup, not the key press. The probe credited an autoplay change to the key. There is no single-character shortcut, so 2.1.4 does not fail.
skeptic: The finding says pressing 'I' with focus on the body changes the page. I replayed it on the live page at 1280x800 and 320x256 with a listener on keydown, keypress and keyup. 'I', 'i' and Shift+I reach the body unhandled (defaultPrevented false), scroll does not move, and repeated presses changed 0 px. When pixels did change, they changed equally on no-key control waits and on other letters: the hero carousel autoplay, the animated floating 'Faça seu agendamento' button and the top banner region. The only document key listeners come from Bootstrap's delegated handlers and the theme's Escape handler for the mobile side nav. No single-character shortcut exists, so the probe attributed a periodic animation to the key press.

auditor: The element is the 'African American Civil War Memorial' result card (a link). I re-ran a Tab walk on the live page (2026-10-23, Edge headless, 1280x800). The pixels right next to the outline on the outside are #eaeaea to #f6f6f6, which gives 2.66 to 2.96:1. Inside, it borders the photo (light sky or water at about 1.6 to 2.1:1) and, only along the bottom, the black text panel. The Understanding document says an outline drawn outside a component has to contrast with the background it sits on, and here that background is below 3:1 everywhere next to the indicator. skeptic: Result card link (African American Civil War Memorial). The Understanding document for 1.4.11 says that a 3D drop shadow is subsumed into the color closest to it in brightness, which here is the white background, and that an outer indicator needs to contrast with the background the component is on. auditor: The header Search button. I logged the focus events live in headless Edge. A Tab from 'Sign in' fires focus on button.search_btn, and in the same millisecond blur on it and focus on input#search_input, while the search menu opens (aria-expanded=true). So the button's focus handler moves focus to another control without any activation. Understanding 3.2.1 lists 'focus is changed to another component when that component receives focus' as a change of context on focus, so this fails 3.2.1 as reported.
